text: 7:15 a.m. The boss texts: “You up? Got a minute?” It arrived while you were brushing your teeth. Answer right now?
The boss's stand-up started with “literally five minutes.” Forty minutes in, he's still talking about his hiking trip. Play along?
A 9:00 meeting from the boss pops up in your calendar. Title: “Let's talk.” No description. It's an hour and a half away. Ask what it's about?
The CEO unexpectedly shows up at your team's morning meeting and sits in the corner. Your boss nods at you nervously: you're presenting, and you're first.
The boss wants “your top three priorities for the week” every Monday. Today you have eleven. Cut it down to three?
The VP catches you at the turnstile: “So glad you're here! Help me carry the awards for the ceremony.” There are thirty boxes of certificates.
Email from the boss at 6:52 a.m. Subject: “URGENT!!!” Body: “Stop by when you get in.” No details. Run over with your coat still on?
The boss announces: team KPIs will now be based on an “engagement index.” Not even he knows how to calculate it. Ask in front of everyone?
left: Stay quiet, figure it out later

text: The CEO's assistant calls at 8:20: “He'll see you at nine. Bring a notepad.” You haven't owned a notepad since high school. Where do you get one?
The boss has introduced pre-meeting exercise: ten squats, whole team, he counts out loud and watches. Join in?
A poster went up over your desk with a quote from the boss: “Impossible is just not done yet.” His name is bigger than the quote. What do you do?
left: Turn it to face the wall

text: The boss is late to his own stand-up and posts in the chat: “Start without me, you run it.” Take charge of the meeting?
The board meets today. The boss asks everyone to “look professional.” You're wearing a hoodie with a cat in a hat on it. Change?
The boss posts a photo of your empty desk at 8:58 in the team chat: “Where is everyone?” The workday starts at nine. React?
Performance reviews are here. The self-assessment asks you to describe “your three superpowers,” at least a paragraph each. How do you fill it out?
The CEO is at the entrance handing out apples “for your health” and asking everyone how they're doing. There's a line of polite people. Join it?
The boss invites you to a breakfast meeting at 8:00 at the café by the office. Says it's on him. Usually that means “split it.” Go?
Morning memo from leadership: the company has new values. There are seven, and by Friday everyone must recite them by heart. Learn them?
This morning the VP and your boss gave you two contradictory assignments. Each is sure his is more important. What now?
The boss, rushing to the elevator: “Oh, you love presentations, right? Great!” The doors close. What just happened?
The boss sent a “Daily Sync” invite for 8:30. Recurs every day until 2099. Accept?
The CEO recorded a 17-minute video address. Below it: “Tell us what inspired you.” Comments are public. Write one?
Monday morning. The boss walks in: “So I was thinking over the weekend.” The team freezes: last weekend spawned three new reports. Listen?
At 8:45 your pay stub arrives. There's a bonus, but exactly half of what was promised at the last meeting. Go ask the boss?
Morning rumor: the boss is getting promoted and looking for a successor. Today, for the first time, he said “good morning” to you first. A sign?
The boss wants a report “in the same format as last time.” Last time he approved three different formats. Ask which one?
Morning rounds: the boss strolls between desks with his mug, peeking at monitors. You've got a beach vacation deals tab open. Close it?
You bring in your vacation request. The boss looks at the calendar and sighs like you asked for a kidney. Insist on your dates?
The boss forwards you a forty-email thread with a note: “Take a look.” At what, exactly, is unclear. What do you do?
Leadership declared a “no-complaints week”: every complaint costs a coin in the jar. By 9 a.m. the jar already has two of yours. Keep going?
The boss is late and looking for someone to blame: “Who even put the stand-up at nine?” He did, a month ago. Remind him?
The CEO hosts a “morning coffee with leadership”: ask anything. Everyone drinks coffee in silence. Ask about cost-of-living raises?
New KPI from the VP: “percentage of positive faces at stand-up.” He'll count them himself, from photos. Start smiling in advance?
You're on a packed subway car. The boss video-calls to “quickly show you one spreadsheet.” Pick up?
“Got a minute?” the boss asks at your desk. His minutes usually last an hour and end with a new task. What do you say?
The boss publicly praises you for a project your coworker actually did. She's sitting right next to you, silent. Correct him?
The boss chews out the whole team for an error in a report. The error is yours, but nobody knows yet. Confess?
The CEO eats in the cafeteria and sits at your table, though there are plenty of free seats. “So, how do you like it here?”
Leadership launches an “Idea of the Week” contest. The best idea gets a certificate. The worst gets implemented by its author. Submit one?
The boss asks you to “check out what the competition is up to.” Deadline: “yesterday.” Scope: “well, you know.” What does that mean?
Your quarterly KPI is growth in a metric that another department calculates and changes. You have zero influence over it. Discuss with the boss?
The board meeting is in hour four. The boss texts from the room: “Need 2017 revenue NOW!” The paper archive is in the basement.
The boss offers a promotion: “Senior Specialist,” same salary, twice the duties. But a new nameplate. Accept?
On the vacation schedule, you and the boss have both claimed the same two weeks in August. He hasn't noticed yet. What do you do?
The VP quietly asks you to prep a brief for him so he can present it before your boss does. Get pulled into office politics?
Anonymous 360 review: you need to rate your boss. Anonymity is handled by his own assistant. Tell the truth?
The boss replies to your nine-point email with one word: “Ok.” What did he approve — everything, or just the greeting?
The CEO messages you directly for the first time. One word: “Come by.” Your direct boss has no idea. Give him a heads-up?
The boss cut the team's office supplies budget to zero and suggested bringing pens from home. He writes with a gold one. What about pens?
The CEO announces a move to a “flat structure, no hierarchy.” An hour later your boss clarifies: he still makes all decisions. Ask a question?
The boss invites you to lunch “to discuss your future.” The whole lunch is about his new car. Your pasta is getting cold. Change the subject?
You have five tasks marked “highest priority.” The boss adds a sixth: “highest priority plus.” Ask him to rank them?
right: Sit with him for an hour

text: The boss chews out the intern in front of the whole team over a typo in a memo. The intern turns red to the ears. Stand up for him?
Leadership invites everyone to team building: kayaking on Saturday. “Voluntary, but we'll remember.” Sign up?
At a meeting the CEO asks: “Who has bold ideas?” Everyone studies the table. Your idea: cancel half of all meetings.
The boss whispers: “Only one person gets a bonus this quarter. I'm rooting for you, but you need to step it up.” Step it up?
The boss asks you to write his birthday message to the CEO. In his name, in verse, and “really heartfelt.” Take it on?
The boss asks you to redo the report “so the numbers look more optimistic.” The numbers themselves won't change. Color the charts green?
The boss is off on a business trip and wants you to be his “eyes and ears”: report who goes to lunch and when. Agree?
New guidelines for emailing leadership: subject, greeting, three points, conclusion. Your two-word email got sent back for revision. Rewrite it?
In the new org chart you were mistakenly assigned to report to two bosses and one meeting room. Raise the issue?
In the kitchen the boss casually dropped: “Changes are coming.” Now the whole team is asking you what changes. You have no idea.
The boss introduced time tracking in 15-minute blocks. Filling it out already takes an hour a day. Log that hour too?
The boss posts “Great work!” in the team chat without saying to whom. Twelve people are typing “Thanks!” at once. You too?
The boss asks you to decide the project's fate because he “trusts you.” If it goes badly, it's your call; if well, it's his. Decide?
The boss suggests you go in his place to an industry conference in another city. You'll have to give a talk. He's already put you on the program.
In a meeting the boss says, “As you and I agreed…” and lays out something you definitely never agreed to. Object?
5:55 p.m. The boss comes out with his laptop: “So, who's not in a hurry?” You already have one arm in your coat.
Saturday, 9 p.m. The boss writes: “Not to bother you, just a thought for Monday.” Fourteen more thoughts follow.
At 6:30 p.m. the boss announces: the CEO visits tomorrow and the office must “shine.” The cleaner already left. Wipe down every desk?
The boss left at 5 p.m. “for a meeting.” Judging by his status photo, the meeting is at a lake house by the grill. Leave early too?
Your performance review results arrive in the evening: “meets expectations.” Apparently the expectations were modest. Dispute it?
At 6:40 p.m. the boss calls you in and offers a promotion. The catch: moving to the branch across town. An hour and a half commute. Accept?
The board meeting got moved to tomorrow, and they want the materials “expanded and shortened at the same time.” It's 6:10 p.m.
Friday, 6 p.m. The boss announces a “quick weekly retro” with pizza. The pizza's on him; the takeaways are on you. Stay?
The team is chipping in for the boss's birthday gift. You're in charge of collecting; three of twelve have paid. The party's tomorrow. What now?
The night before your vacation. The boss asks you to “stay reachable, only for the most urgent stuff.” His most urgent stuff happens twice a day.
Sunday, 7 p.m. The boss calls “for literally a minute” to get the shared folder password. It's at the office, and you're at a barbecue.
At 6:20 p.m. the CEO walks the floor turning off lights to save energy. You're still working in the far corner. Speak up?
Late in the day the boss sends you an angry ALL-CAPS email and CCs the whole team. Reply all or just to him?
End of the month, two closed tasks short of your KPI. You could close two old ones nobody needs. The boss is “fine with it, if done smart.”
Friday, 7:30 p.m. The boss writes: “Think about strategy over the weekend. No pressure.” Then books a meeting for Saturday at 9:00.
Unwritten team rule: nobody leaves before the boss. It's 7:10 p.m., and he's in his office watching a show. Say goodbye?
left: Sit as long as he does

text: At an evening staff event the CEO raises a toast “to those who work weekends.” Join the toast?
At 6:45 p.m. the boss asks for the weekly report “in a nutshell.” You write two words, and he wants it “more detailed, a page.” Now?
Leadership is paying for a “Leadership for Everyone” course. Evenings, three times a week, for six months. Sign up?
The CEO announced annual bonuses. Yours is a voucher for “an evening with leadership” at the bowling alley. Go?
On his way out, the boss sticks a note on your monitor: “Do this by morning, it's easy.” The task: rewrite the team's entire rulebook.
The boss is on a beach vacation but every evening at 7 he gathers the team on video “for five minutes.” Waves crash in the background. Join?
In the evening the boss asks you, “as a friend,” to name the worst worker on the team. He won't accept “nobody.”
The promotion you were counting on went to the son of the CEO's friend. The boss asks you to “help the kid settle in.” Help?
Your vacation starts tomorrow, and the request still isn't signed. The boss is in a meeting “until end of day.” Catch him at the door?
The boss invites you to dinner with company partners. Your role: “just be there and nod occasionally.” Dinner's at 8 p.m., out of town.
Friday, 5:40 p.m. The boss scheduled a meeting “to review this week's meetings.” Attendance mandatory. Try to get out of it?
At 10:15 p.m. the boss puts a “+” under your three-day-old message. Approval, a hint, or a slipped finger?
In the evening the CEO sends an email: “We are one family.” Attached: new overtime policies. Reply to it?
Saturday, 6 p.m. The boss sends a photo of a store shelf: “Is this the competitor's product? Find out the price ASAP.” You're at a friend's birthday.
6:05 p.m. Before leaving, everyone must name “one win of the day.” Your win: surviving until 6:05.
The boss walks you to the elevator, tossing out tasks for tomorrow. The elevator has come three times already. Step in mid-sentence?
At an evening meeting the CEO praises your team but mixes it up with Accounting. Accounting is already applauding itself. Correct him?
8:40 a.m. A courier with signed contracts is stuck at the front desk: nobody ordered him a pass. Run down for the papers or fill out a 12-field pass form?
At 7:12 a.m. the client sends a nine-minute voice memo: “Looked at the mockup over breakfast, have some thoughts.” Listen now or after coffee?
Email from the paper supplier: “Prices went up 18% as of Monday. The contract? Well, a contract is also just paper.” Going to argue?
The office renovation contractor promised to come “in the morning.” It's 11:40 and he texts: “Close by, forty minutes.” Wait or find another crew?
The tender bid is due by 10:00, but the e-signature is on a USB stick with the accountant, who's on a beach vacation. Call the beach?
The morning starts with an online review: “Awful service, but the manager was sweet.” The manager is you. Reply publicly?
Partners land for 9:30 negotiations, but Accounting took the meeting room for the annual audit with three boxes of binders. Kick them out?
The client's email starts with “Good morning! Quick question:” followed by 34 numbered points. Answer every one?
The coffee supplier brought a trial batch of beans “for the whole team.” In return he wants a signature on a paper that looks suspiciously like a yearly contract.
Expo morning. The organizer hands you the costume of the company mascot: a life-size plush stapler. Put it on?
8:05 a.m. The delivery courier calls: the client's samples are outside the office, but the office is still locked. Head in early?
The “final” spec arrived. File name: Spec_final_REALLY_final_v7_Olegs_edits.docx. Nobody knows who Oleg is. Investigate?
left: Work with the file as is

text: The contract designer announces a creative block: mockups will come “when inspiration strikes.” The client presentation is Thursday.
The client's Accounting sent a reconciliation: you owe them 12 cents. They want it paid by lunch. Do it officially?
Foreign partners came for a breakfast meeting, but the interpreter is sick. Your language skills: “Where is the library?” level. Lead the talk?
The office supplier delivered 50 pallets of paper instead of 50 reams. The driver wants the invoice signed, or he'll dump it all at the entrance.
A big client's procurement wants a vendor questionnaire: 140 questions, including “your director's favorite color.” Fill it out honestly?
Two hours to the client demo, and the deck exists only on the laptop of an intern who's away on a business trip. What now?
In your inbox: a contract to sign from a “new supplier” writing as if everything's already agreed. You've never heard of this company.
A 9:00 meeting “at our office.” The office turns out to be in a business park out of town: five identical buildings, no signs. Find it yourself?
The cleaning company billed you for “cleanup after the office party.” There was no party. Or there was, and you weren't invited. Look into it?
First thing in the morning, a partner congratulates you on “your professional holiday.” You have no idea what holiday that is. Return the favor?
The bank's call center: “Your call is very important to us.” Minute 47 on hold, and you need the bank letter for the tender by lunch. Keep waiting?
Morning email from a client in Tokyo: “Needed it yesterday, but our lunchtime works.” Their lunch starts in half an hour.
You walk in and a contractor's rep is already sitting in the meeting room: “They told me to wait here.” Who told him is a mystery. Offer tea?
The supplier's shipment is stuck in customs: the declaration says “parts (various).” Call a customs broker?
The client wants a proposal “in a format that's easy to read on a smartwatch.” It's morning; the coffee hasn't kicked in.
Morning traffic jam, and your bag holds the original contracts the client must sign by 10:00. Their office is a mile away. Run?
The conference organizer says your talk was cut from twenty minutes to four. You have 46 slides. Rework it?
The water jugs arrived, but yesterday the old vendor took the cooler away “for unpaid bills.” There's water, but no cooler. What now?
The client calls back: “I changed my mind. Let's go back to the option I rejected three weeks ago.” That option no longer exists anywhere.
A courier brings flowers from partners with a card: “To our favorite Purchasing team.” You're not Purchasing, but it's a gorgeous bouquet. Keep it?
The ad agency sent a report: “Reach grew 400%!” It went from three people to fifteen. Show it to leadership?
The client lost his voice and asks you to “just for a minute” be his voice in a call with his own bosses. On speakerphone. Agree?
At the meeting the client asks for “wow, but strictly on-brand.” The brand book is one page that says “blue.” Come up with a wow?
The contractor blew the deadline a third time and sent a fruit basket as an apology. Your coworkers are already picking it clean. Cancel the contract?
The client paid the invoice but wrote “for emotional damages” in the payment memo. Accounting refuses to process it. Step in?
Price negotiations. The client's buyer has been silent for two minutes, staring out the window. It's a tactic. Cave and offer a discount?
A visitor grilled you at the booth for half an hour, took all the brochures and pens, and said, “I'm just a student.” The next one is reaching for pens.
The client interrupts on slide two: “Can we skip to the last one?” The last slide is the price, and you haven't explained the value yet.
A courier brings the client's papers: signatures in the wrong spots, stamp upside down, one page from someone else's contract. Send them back?
In the tender, a competitor bid below the price of air. Leadership asks if you can go “a tiny bit lower.” Redo the estimate?
The client demands “all source files,” including your drafts, your meme folder, and your work playlist. Hand it all over?
The ISP's call center asks you to restart the router for the fifth time. You're calling about a billing error. Demand a supervisor?
A partner offers a barter: you build his website, he mentions you on social media. He has 112 followers, half of them relatives.
The client asks you to send “your most creative person” to the next meeting. The whole team looks at you. You look at the intern.
The video studio's estimate has a line item: “Camera operator's mood: $200.” Everything else looks fair. Haggle?
The supplier wants you to sign a 30-page amendment where everything that used to be in big print is now in fine print. Read it all?
The client asks to “move the deadline a bit.” Earlier. A week earlier, because “that's how it worked out.” Agree?
Edits arrived as a photo of a printout: everything circled in pen, with a note: “here.” Call the client to decode it?
At a conference you're dropped into a panel in place of a sick speaker. Topic: “The Industry in 50 Years.” You'd prepared for the coffee break.
The client wants a clause in the contract: “The contractor is always reachable.” Always means nights and vacations too. Sign?
The client accidentally posts in the project chat a message calling you “our sweet slowpoke.” Pretend you didn't notice?
A supplier gives you a branded blanket and planner “as a token of future cooperation.” The supply tender is next week. Accept?
The contract developer delivered. Everything works, but only while he's standing next to it watching the screen. Accept the work?
The client opens his laptop to show you “how it should be done”: your main competitor's website. That one. What do you say?
New review of the company: “Ordered from them in 2009, still think about it.” Whether that's good or bad is unclear. Reply?
The client orders “the same as last time, only different.” Details: “You're the pros, you'll figure it out.”
The supplier invoiced in dollars, euros, and mysterious “units.” The amounts differ in every currency. Pay it?
The courier service lost the contract with original signatures. The operator suggests you “check a branch in another city.”
A prospective client wants a free “trial” project to gauge your skills. The trial project is the entire project.
The partner arrives at negotiations with a lawyer, an accountant, and his mom. Mom asks the toughest questions. Answer her directly?
An intern handles approvals on the client side: he approves everything in three seconds, then his boss shows up and cancels it all. Go over his head?
A vendor translated the deck for a foreign client. The “Our Values” slide became “Our Prices.” Check the rest?
The print shop ran 5,000 business cards for the client with a typo in his last name. You made the typo. Confess?
As thanks, a client sent the team 90 pounds of his own frozen dumplings. The office fridge fits three bags.
At the product demo for the client, everything worked perfectly. That's scarier than any crash. Sign the acceptance right now?
6:40 p.m. You accidentally open the client's message, it shows “Read,” and instantly: “Oh, you're online!” Reply?
In the evening the contractor sends a photo of the finished expo booth. The company name is misspelled, and the booth is already on its way.
5:55 p.m. The client sent the signed contract: scanned upside down, missing the last page. Accounting leaves at 6:00 sharp.
An evening call from a supplier: “Customer success here, a service quality survey, just twenty minutes.” Finally a chance to speak your mind. Answer?
The client invites you to celebrate the signed deal at a restaurant. Tonight at 7:30, across town. Go?
6:20 p.m. A partner on the phone: “Let me quickly explain, you take notes.” Quickly means fifty minutes, and your pen just died.
A huge branded gift basket arrives from a partner. Nothing edible inside, just thirty logo pens. Share with coworkers?
7 p.m. The client sends the “absolutely final” edit. At 7:04, another one, “the very last.” Make them one at a time?
The conference is over; the reception and networking begin. You need to hand out fifty business cards. You have four, one with a coffee stain.
The client left a review: “Everything's great, but three stars so you don't get lazy.” Ask him to change the rating?
6:30 p.m. The contractor: “It's done, but you get it only after payment.” Accounting pays only after delivery. Full circle.
6:05 p.m. You call the client about payment. He says: “The money's been sent.” Sent where, he won't say.
In the evening, an invite to a tender with bids due by 9:00 tomorrow. You need 14 certificates, two of which are only issued on Wednesdays.
5:45 p.m. The client sends an email with 27 people CC'd, including your CEO. Reply all?
The expo closed and the booth needs taking down. The installers left at 5 p.m. “per contract.” It's you, a screwdriver, and a 10x20 ft banner.
right: Take it down with a pal

text: 6:10 p.m. The supplier asks you to confirm the order now, “or the price goes up tomorrow.” He's said that every evening for a month.
In the evening the client sends a reference: “I want it like this.” It's your own project, which he rejected a year ago.
6:30 p.m. A partner asks for the company's “latest” deck. The latest is two years old and still shows the old office.
The client calls in the evening from his personal phone, steam hissing in the background. Wants an invoice right now, “while I'm in a good mood.”
6:15 p.m. The courier came for the papers before you printed them. The printer's on another floor, and the courier has “forty more stops.”
The caterer for the client's event tomorrow reports: the chef quit and took the food with him. The event starts tomorrow at noon.
A client left you a personal five-star review but got your name wrong. Now the whole team is congratulating some guy named Arkady.
6:00 p.m.: “We won't sign, the lawyer objects.” 6:20 p.m.: “We'll sign, the lawyer went home.” Sign before the lawyer's back?
In the evening the client asks to bill a different entity, then a third, or better yet, split it into four parts of 25%. Redo it?
On your way out, a supplier's rep catches you: he “was in the area and decided to drop by” with a 300-page catalog.
Evening call to the delivery service. The operator transfers you to a specialist, who offers to transfer you back to the operator.
Evening presentation at the client's. Their projector shows everything green, and your brand color is red. How do you wriggle out?
6:40 p.m. The photographer sent 1,200 shots from the client's event and wants you to pick the best “since you know better.”
At the end of the day, a competitor's rep calls offering to switch you to their services. He apparently doesn't know where you work. Chat?
5:40 p.m. The client asks to duplicate the documents “just in case”: zipped, unzipped, and by fax. The office hasn't had a fax in ten years.
Wednesday evening. The client writes: “I had an idea for the weekend.” The weekend is two days away and he's already planning it for you.
6:30 p.m. The supplier thanks you for the partnership and attaches a $5 invoice for the “thank-you letter.” Pay it?
A partner suggests discussing a big deal “in an informal setting”: at his country house on Saturday, with a sauna and barbecue.
An 87-question engagement survey. Question one: “How happy are you, 1 to 10?” Anonymity guaranteed, but your last name is in the link. Answer?
At 8:45 the onboarding bot cheerfully asks how your first week is going and offers a “Find the Kitchen” quest. You've worked here six years. Play along?
Starting Monday, the dress code is “smart casual with touches of corporate blue.” Your entire wardrobe is shades of gray. What now?
A poster above your desk: “Today is the best day to outdo yourself!” The man on it smiles right at you all day long. Move it?
At 9:00 sharp the PA starts the company morning workout. Coworkers wave their arms awkwardly by their monitors. Join in?
Your photo appeared on the lobby wall of fame captioned “Team Veteran.” It's your ten-year-old badge photo, with bangs. Ask to replace it?
HR asks everyone at the door to name one of the company's five values out loud. You only remember “Customer-centricity” and that there are five.
They're handing out company hoodies for a group photo. Only XS and XXXL are left. HR insists: everyone in hoodies today. Wear one?
You've been made a buddy for a new hire. By 9:30 he's asked 14 questions, including “where are the outlets” and “what's the meaning of our company.”
Your throat hurts. The sick-leave portal wants a doctor's note, a scan, a selfie with a thermometer, and three approvals. Or you could just go in.
The morning bot asks: “How's your mood?” with three faces. Rumor is, click the sad one and the team psychologist is dispatched to you at once.
Mandatory time-management training starts at 9:00 and runs four hours. Nobody canceled your tasks for the day, of course. What now?
The new HR director holds a meet-and-greet and asks everyone for a fun fact about themselves. The line is creeping toward you.
You got a five-year personal development plan. The “Goal” field is pre-filled: “Become even more engaged.” Sign it?
HR introduced hot desking: first come, first served for window seats. It's 8:10, and coworkers are already sprinting down the hall with backpacks.
The company “10,000 Steps a Day” challenge kicks off. The leaderboard hangs in the lobby, and your team is dead last.
An anonymous suggestion box went up in the lobby. Directly above it: a camera. Drop in a note about the broken coffee machine?
New hires get a welcome kit: mug, notebook, and logo socks. Old-timers, it turns out, get nothing. Ask for a kit?
At 9:00 HR ceremoniously congratulates this month's birthdays over the PA. They mispronounced your name, and coworkers are already trying it out.
By lunch you must enter next year's vacations into the shared calendar. The best summer weeks get snapped up in minutes. Act now?
HR launches corporate English classes at 8 a.m. Lesson one: how to say “synergy” with confident intonation.
You must take a “What Color Is Your Personality” test. The result goes on a sign at your desk. Everyone around is a “green team player.”
HR introduced a “clean desk” policy, and during the morning check your beloved cat mug went into the “Unclaimed” box. Get it back?
HR asks: “How likely are you to recommend the company to a friend?” Your best friend, by the way, quit here last year.
Company 5K run on Saturday. HR goes desk to desk with a list: “You're in, right? We already printed a T-shirt with your name.”
HR introduced a morning “gratitude minute”: everyone publicly thanks a coworker in the chat. It's your turn, and the only one you know is the water cooler.
As part of the “culture of openness,” all meeting room doors were removed. Your quiet call room is now a hallway. Object?
Badges are handed out where you write your “superpower.” Your neighbor has “Fixes printers with a glare,” the accountant: “Never blinks at reports.”
The company psychologist comes once a week. The only open slot is 9:00, in the glass-walled meeting room facing the kitchen.
Your vacation request was returned: signed in blue pen, but it must be black. Vacation's in three days, and HR only accepts forms until 10:00. Run?
“Thank-You Points” launched: coworkers give each other points, redeemable for a pen. Everyone on your team has a hundred points. You have zero.
HR declared a month of theme days: Monday was hat day, Tuesday sock day, and today is pajama day. You're standing at your closet.
The 360 review is on: rate 23 coworkers on 40 competencies by the end of the week. Start this morning with a fresh head?
At the morning all-hands you're handed a certificate “For Five Years of Loyalty.” You've been here three, but arguing on stage feels awkward.
Team building: kayaking on Saturday, participation “strictly voluntary.” Your name is already on the roster for boat number three.
At a trust training you must fall backward into coworkers' arms. Catching you: the accountant who dropped his laptop this morning. Fall?
A mandatory three-hour webinar: “Emotional Intelligence in the Digital Age.” Cameras on, because “engagement matters.”
Charity bake sale: everyone bakes a pie, proceeds go to a dog shelter. You have no recipes and no oven. How do you take part?
Invitation to “lunch with HR, just to talk.” Lunch is free, but at the end you have to name three growth areas for your team.
The coworker from the next row was “set free to explore new opportunities.” HR asks you not to discuss it and hands you his tasks. How do you react?
Contest: “My Workday in One Photo.” The winner will be shown on the lobby screen; the prize is a branded thermos. Enter?
In your 360 report an anonymous coworker writes: “Chews apples loudly.” There are four people on the team, and only one of them eats apples.
New mugs with company values were handed out. Yours says “Speed,” and it leaks. Your neighbor has a dry “Calm” mug.
Dress code raid. You're in sneakers, but “closed-toe business shoes” are required. Under the next desk: someone's dress shoes, two sizes too big.
A ping-pong table was set up in the office “for decompression.” Coworkers invite you to a game, but management eyes the table with deep suspicion.
The learning portal says 12 mandatory courses are overdue. Each ends with a test and a certificate nobody ever looks at.
It's “Bring Your Kids to Work Day.” Someone's son is drawing a dinosaur right over your project plan on the whiteboard. Step in?
HR is looking for talent show participants. Your team unanimously nominates you because you “hummed in the elevator once.”
HR asks you to run a workshop for the whole office on “What We Actually Do Here.” It starts in an hour; you have zero slides.
A departing coworker asks for a reference for his new employer's HR. He worked, to put it mildly, in power-saving mode.
New rule: every department must give one person a “below expectations” rating. A suspiciously polite silence falls over the office.
The company merch store opens. Everyone gets 300 points; the cheapest item is a 450-point keychain. Go complain?
Healthy Eating Week: the cookies are gone from the kitchen, replaced by celery. Your coworkers stare at the celery with quiet hatred.
HR wants a “success story” for the company newsletter: two pages, inspiring tone, facts optional. Due by lunch.
Secret Santa kicks off. You drew the CFO, whom you've seen exactly once, in an elevator. Gift limit: $10.
HR posts the anonymous survey results, broken down by department, age, and favorite color. You're the only orange fan in the department.
HR wants everyone posting weekly on the internal social network. Your feed is empty; your neighbor posted his lunch: “Living our values.”
You're offered a spot in the “Future Leaders Academy”: six months of Saturday classes. Graduates are promised “expanded responsibilities.”
The office opens a “recharge zone” with a hammock. It's free, but it hangs by the glass wall of the room where the execs are meeting.
At the office health checkup, the eye doctor prescribes “reduced screen time.” HR clarifies: it's a recommendation, not an exemption.
Volunteer day: plant trees outside the building instead of lunch. Shovels are signed out, and the photographer is already here.
HR assigned you a mentor. He's two years younger and first advises you to “reflect more and keep a gratitude journal.”
The internal job board lists an opening in a team with windows and no morning stand-ups. HR warns: everyone will know you applied.
“Blind lunch”: random pairs of employees grab lunch together. Your match is a lawyer who speaks only in contract clauses.
“Coziest Desk” contest, prize: pizza for the team. Your neighbors have fairy lights and pillows; you have a stack of printouts. Decorate?
The newsletter is interviewing the “most senior employee on the team.” Surprise: that's you. Question: “Where do you see yourself here in 20 years?”
HR's lunchtime “open door hour”: ask the HR director anything. The question about cost-of-living raises hangs in the air. Ask it?
The office party theme is the Roaring Twenties: feathers, vests, pearls. Your closet holds only jeans, and the bus leaves in two hours. Improvise?
right: Sew a costume from a curtain

text: At the party the emcee yells: “Karaoke time! First up, our shyest employee!” For some reason he's looking at you.
At the party the CEO asks someone to toast the company values. Everyone stares at their plates — and you accidentally stare at the CEO.
Company history trivia night at 6 p.m. Your department's team is one player short without you.
A coworker is leaving and invites everyone to farewell tea at 5:30. HR asks people “not to linger or make a thing of it.”
Collecting money for the HR director's big birthday. The amount is “suggested,” and the list of who paid hangs on the kitchen door.
Training at 6 p.m.: “How to Say No.” To skip it, you'd have to say no to HR, which you can't do yet. A vicious circle.
Evening team-building at the bowling alley: whoever bowls a strike becomes captain. The ball seems heavier than it looks.
5:55 p.m. You must fill in the whole month's timesheet by 6:00. You only remember today, and not all of it.
The party has a photo booth with props, and the photos go straight to the company-wide chat. Coworkers tug at your sleeve.
HR is forming a “corporate culture task force.” Meetings Wednesdays at 6:30 p.m., cookies at your own expense. Join?
The new hire's probation is ending, and HR needs your review by 6 p.m. The new hire is standing behind you, trying to breathe quietly.
After-work lecture: “Financial Literacy for Employees.” The speaker advises saving 30% of your salary. The room laughs nervously.
Party game: pass an orange without hands, tucked under your chin. Your partner is the chief accountant in a stiff suit.
At the party, the head of HR asks you to slow dance to a song about “one big happy family.” Everyone is watching.
The party is winding down. HR hands out an “Rate the Event” survey to fill out right now, “while it's fresh.”
Board game night at 6:30. In the economy game, a guy from Accounting already owns half the map and is gloating.
At the exit, HR hands out branded umbrellas, but only to those who pose with the logo for social media. It's pouring outside.
5:45 p.m. A coworker was called to HR “with their things.” Ten minutes later in chat: “Dear colleagues, some structural changes…” The team looks at you.
The company soccer team needs a goalie for a match against the office next door. Kickoff at 7 p.m.; the only jersey left is number 13.
HR creates a 400-person chat called “Our Happy Family.” At 6:30 p.m., a flood of “Have a lovely evening, colleagues” e-cards begins.
Your department has to put on a skit at the holiday party. Rehearsals every day after 6 p.m. Who's directing?
At 6 p.m. a bus leaves for an off-site retreat. Agenda: reflection, meditation, and a 6 a.m. wake-up for “purpose workouts.”
6:05 p.m., you're at the elevator. HR catches you “for a sec”: fill out a form for the “Wall of Faces” with a favorite quote and a baby photo.
right: Go back and fill it out

text: At 6 p.m. the company book club discusses “How to Love Mondays.” All you know about the book is its cover.
Intern farewell party. HR asks you to say something inspiring to each of the ten. It's 6:40 p.m. and you've never seen them before.
“Employee of the Year” nominations. You must nominate someone from your team. Not yourself — though you'd really like to. Now what?
right: Hint your neighbor to pick you

text: It's a coworker's last day. HR asks you to get the team to sign a card by 6 p.m., but half the team works remotely.
New rule: no work chat messages after 7 p.m., “for balance.” It's 6:59, and a coworker is really waiting for your reply.
Evening clay workshop: “Sculpt a Company Value.” Your “Transparency” looks suspiciously like an ashtray.
Party raffle: grand prize is a day off; consolation prize is the honor of organizing the next party. Tickets cost $3.
HR asks you to stay after 6 p.m. to film a “Why I Love My Job” video. Smile, speak from the heart, as many takes as needed.
6:15 p.m., HR calls: they want you to move your vacation “because it's a critical period.” Your beach tickets were bought ages ago.
The turnstile blinks red: your badge got demagnetized. Behind you, a line of Accounting with hot coffee. The guard left “for a minute” twenty minutes ago.
The elevator arrives packed, but a coworker by the buttons waves you in: “You'll fit if you don't breathe.” Fourteen floors to go. Squeeze in?
Since morning the coffee machine demands: “Empty grounds container.” It's been full since yesterday, and the line is watching to see who caves first.
right: Clean it in front of everyone

text: One spot left in the lot: between a pillar and a crookedly parked SUV. Your side mirrors are visibly nervous. Risk it?
Overnight, your chair got swapped for a squeaky one with a broken armrest. Yours, with your sticker on it, is at a desk in the next department. Reclaim it?
The office manager meets you at the door with a survey: “Which cookies should we order next quarter?” 38 options, every field required. Fill it out?
Someone flung the window open “for fresh air.” It's 17°F outside, your desk is right under it, and papers flutter across the office like pigeons. Close it?
There's someone's mug on your desk with half-drunk tea and a film on top. Owner unknown, but someone's forgotten badge lies next to it. Investigate?
left: Quietly take it to the kitchen
right: Post a photo in team chat

text: Someone boiled eggs in the office kettle: the shells on the bottom prove it, and the water smells like breakfast. There's no other kettle on the floor.
right: Scrub it and post a note

text: Your badge is at home in your other jacket. Security will issue a temp one, but it needs your manager's signature, and your manager is stuck in traffic.
The office manager hands everyone a plant “for coziness.” You get a cactus with a tag: “My name is Gennady. Water on Thursdays.” Adopt him?
The courier brought your breakfast oatmeal, but security won't let him past reception. Going down means being late to the stand-up.
It's “Health Month”: before 10 a.m. the elevator stops only on even floors. You work on the seventh. How will you get up?
You booked the meeting room for 9:00, but three people from the next department are already in there, carefully not seeing the calendar. Kick them out?
The light over your desk is dying and flashing like a disco. Facilities requests take five business days. Now what?
right: Stand on a chair, unscrew it

text: The coat rack by the door is full: someone hung three jackets and a big umbrella on your hook. Meanwhile your wet jacket drips onto your shoes.
The water cooler bottle is empty. A new five-gallon one sits next to it, and everyone walking by is staring very intently at their phones. Your move?
The cleaner is mopping the aisle to your desk and says sternly: “Not on my clean floor!” The detour goes through the executives' office.
The office manager announces: at noon the fridge gets cleared out completely. Deep inside sits your container from last week. Or something that used to be yours.
right: Pull it out and wash it

text: The kitchen now has five recycling bins with fine-print labels. You're holding a cup: paper, plastic, and a lid of mysterious composition.
The office switched to hot-desking. At 9:05 the only free desks are by the bathroom door and under the PA speaker. Where do you settle?
Reception has a mountain of boxes, and one is yours — a personal order, new curtains. The box is your size, only wider. Haul it across the office?
Your desk has one outlet and you have three chargers. Your neighbor offers a power strip in exchange for parking his space heater under your desk.
New pod coffee machine, with rations: five pods per person per week. It's Monday and you already want your third. Where do you get coffee?
Security is replacing badges and photographing everyone right at the turnstile. Overhead lighting, you just got off the subway, and this photo stays with you for five years.
The morning sun is blasting your monitor. One cord controls the blinds for the whole row, and your neighbor by the window adores “natural light.”
There's a big jar of jam in the kitchen with a note: “Help yourselves!” The jam is suspiciously brown, and all the clean spoons are in the sink.
A memo on your desk: “Pens are issued against signature, one per quarter.” Yours ran out yesterday. How will you sign anything?
Your locker key snapped off in the lock. Inside: your office shoes, your charger, and a strategic half sandwich. Facilities won't be in till lunch.
right: Pick the lock with a ruler

text: The parking gate doesn't recognize your plate. Three cars honk behind you, and the guard says on the intercom: “Repeat the plate number. Slowly.”
left: Turn around, park on the street

text: Someone put an “Ocean Breeze” diffuser in the open office. By 10 a.m. the whole floor smells like a taxi air freshener. Remove the source?
You biked in, but the bike rack is blocked with old chairs. Security suggests locking your bike to the palm tree in the lobby.
The cleaners took the box under your desk: slippers, a blanket, and a cookie stash. Trash pickup is at 10 a.m. Run to the rescue?
The entrance has facial recognition now. It insists you're a courier and keeps sending you to the loading dock. Argue with a machine?
The printer is printing your 40-page contract but munches every third page with an appetizing crunch. You need it by 3 p.m.
left: Print one page at a time

text: Seven people in line for the microwave. First up: a coworker with fish that's been reheating for eight minutes. Will you wait?
Your yogurt, labeled in marker, vanished from the fridge. In the trash: the empty cup with your name on it. Launch an investigation?
You need half an hour of quiet, but every meeting room is taken. Only “The Closet” is free: an old supply room with one chair and a cardboard smell.
The AC above you drips on a strict schedule: every eight seconds, on the same spot — right on your desk. What will you do?
The courier gave you someone else's lunch: a huge double-cheese burger instead of your salad. He's gone, and the burger's owner hasn't turned up.
The restroom on your floor is under repair; the nearest working one is by Accounting, one floor down. The line there has its own hierarchy.
right: Go up to the execs' floor

text: The office scanner emails files to someone who quit two years ago. Today it sent him the scan of your passport for your badge.
The monstera in the corner has grown so big it blocks the way to the window. The office manager needs a volunteer to repot it. Step up?
The kitchen has six seats and twelve hungry people. Your tablemates discuss their diets so loudly your appetite melts away.
The coffee machine displayed “Error 47” and went silent. The manual is in a mystery language, and the whole floor stares at it in grief. Go inside?
right: Take it apart by the pictures

text: The team has one stapler, and it's chained to the office manager's desk. You need to staple forty sets of documents.
The printer's out of paper. The supply is locked in a cabinet, the office manager has the key, and she's at lunch until 3.
The office next door is being renovated. The hammer drill kicks in at the exact moment a good idea arrives.
Your chair's gas lift gave up: every ten minutes you slowly sink until you're at desk level. What now?
The office manager wants a photo of your desk for the “Clean Desk” contest. You have fourteen mugs and a receipt from two years ago.
The AC remote is missing. Turns out your neighbor keeps it in his drawer and hands it out strictly “by appointment.” Book a slot?
The elevator is stuck between floors. With you: two people from the next department and a courier with a huge bag of fragrant dumplings. It'll be a while.
The bin under your desk hasn't been emptied in three days. The cleaner insists anything under desks is the employees' responsibility.
right: Take out the whole row's trash

text: The best meeting room is booked for the next month by a recurring meeting called “Reserved.” Per the directory, its owner quit long ago.
Reception asks you to take a package for your deskmate. The box weighs as much as a washing machine and gurgles suspiciously. Take it?
The office manager is on vacation and left you a watering schedule for twelve plants. Each has its own name, water quota, and personality.
A window washer hangs outside on a platform, reading your monitor with great interest. Judging by his bucket, he's here all day.
One kettle for forty people. You put water on, stepped away for a minute — and it's already been poured into other people's mugs.
Ahead of you at the printer, a coworker is printing a 300-page manual. Your document is one page, and you need it right now.
The office manager is taking supply orders: one item per team. You've long dreamed of a decent mouse pad; the team wants whiteboard markers.
A mountain of dirty mugs sits in the sink, and a “Dish Duty Schedule” hangs on the wall. Today's name on the schedule is yours.
Your neighbor plugged a heater, a kettle, and a lamp into one power strip under your desk. It's starting to smell quietly alarming.
The building cafeteria has a 20-minute line, and the office vending machine has only crab-flavored chips and a bar on its expiration date.
A desk phone on an empty desk has rung every five minutes since morning. The ringtone: a peppy polka. Pick up?
It's “Clean Office Day”: each team turns in a bag of unneeded papers. You have no unneeded papers, only “what if I need it.”
Someone burned popcorn in the microwave. The whole floor smells of smoke, and for some reason everyone's looking at you.
The office manager bought new coffee “with notes of prune and cardboard.” The old beans are locked in the “guests only” cabinet.
5:59 p.m. The exit turnstile froze, there's a crowd at the door, and the guard announces: “One at a time, manually, by list.”
In the evening you find your soup in the fridge, and there's nothing at home. Hauling a container of broth on the subway is a dubious adventure.
right: Eat the soup in the kitchen

text: At 6 p.m. the whole building crowds the elevators. Each car arrives already full from the top floors — fifth time in a row.
After 6 p.m. energy saving kicks in: lights go off if nobody moves for five minutes. You're finishing an email and waving your arms every four.
The cleaner arrives to vacuum your row right when you decided to “quickly finish one thing.” The vacuum is loud and very persistent.
Someone's blocked your car in. No note, no phone number — just a sticker on the windshield: “Be right back.”
The kitchen is emptying, and the trash bag is overflowing and suspiciously leaking. The cleaner won't be in until tomorrow. Whose problem is this?
Before the weekend, the office manager asks people to take plants home: the heat's off for two days. You got a dracaena as tall as a first grader.
You've got your jacket on, but a window is wide open on the floor, and a downpour is starting. Security doesn't come up after 6.
left: Not your window, not your rain

text: You're staying late and ordered dinner to the office, but the courier went to the building's other tower and wants you to come there.
You pop into a meeting room for your forgotten charger and find an after-hours cake party. They invite you in “for literally a minute.”
Before leaving, you find your mug missing from the drying rack. In its place is someone else's, labeled “Not mine, don't touch.”
Your umbrella is gone from the shared stand by the door, and it's pouring. One umbrella is left — pink, kid-sized, with ears.
left: Run to the subway in the rain

text: 5:40 p.m. The office manager announces an inventory: everyone must find the asset tags on their monitor, chair, and stapler.
You printed your personal gym pool application, but the default printer turned out to be on the executive floor. The page is sitting in the tray.
In the evening the AC suddenly switches to “sauna” mode, and it can only be turned off from the main panel at the security desk downstairs.
5:30 p.m. The office manager reminds everyone: leave papers on your desk and your monitor gets a “Cleanliness Violator” sticker.
The microwave has been beeping for twenty minutes: someone left soup in it and went home. The beeps echo across the emptying floor.
right: Toss the soup and clean it

text: 6:30 p.m. The guard does his rounds and sternly asks the stragglers: “Gonna be long? I need to lock the floor.” Ask for more time?
left: Beg for half an hour more

text: The floor is being set up for tomorrow's event, and the movers are carrying out desks. Yours too — with documents in the drawer.
right: Chase your desk down the stairs

text: The office manager is sorting the bins and loudly asks who threw batteries in “Plastic.” The batteries are from your mouse.
Your neighbor is going on vacation and offers to swap chairs for two weeks. His is soft, heated, and very easy to fall asleep in.
Your jacket got moved to the back of the coat room, behind forty coats from conference guests. The attendant left at 6 sharp.
Evening email: the kitchen kettle burned out, and the office manager asks everyone to chip in $5 for a new one. Raised: $10. Needed: $50.
Already outside, you realize your badge is on your desk and the floor is alarmed. Without the badge, you won't get in tomorrow.
By 7 the open office empties out and becomes blissfully quiet. But at 8 the company choir rehearses here, and the altos are expecting you.
Someone locked your bike to theirs with their own lock. Nobody at the front desk knows who owns the other bike.
5:55 p.m. A line forms at the floor's only working restroom: everyone with a commute over an hour.
The dishwasher finished its cycle. Putting away clean dishes is the unwritten duty of whoever opens it first. You already opened it.
End-of-day email: “Tomorrow the team moves to another floor. Pack your things by 7 p.m.” They handed out two boxes for everyone.
At the exit, the guard asks to open your backpack: “Random check.” Inside is a pack of cookies from the office kitchen.
Time to return the meeting room key to reception, but the key is inside and the door slammed shut. Reception closes in ten minutes.
The heat turned off at 6 on schedule, and you have half an hour of work left. On the next chair lies a blanket embroidered “MINE.”
The “15-minute” stand-up is in its 50th minute. A coworker is describing what he did yesterday, including details about lunch. Interrupt?
Morning call, cameras on. You're wearing a blazer, and below the frame — pajama pants with reindeer. Turn the camera on?
right: Turn it on, don't stand up

text: Overnight, the team chat piled up 214 unread messages. Read them all or hit “Mark as read”?
At 8:02 a.m. an email arrives titled “URGENT!!!” with an empty body. The sender: the department next door. Call and find out?
The 9:00 meeting is just called “Sync.” No description, no agenda, twelve attendees. What do you do?
At stand-up they ask what you did yesterday. Yesterday was nonstop calls about what should be done. What do you say?
You've been talking for two minutes, and everyone is silently waving at the camera. Your mic is off, of course. Start over?
A coworker sent you a 7-minute-40-second voice message first thing. You're on the subway and left your earbuds at home. Listen anyway?
Your messenger status has said “Online” since last night. The boss writes: “I see you're in, come see me.” You're still on the bus.
Your calendar has three mandatory meetings at 10:00 at once. Each organizer is sure theirs is the important one.
An email with seventeen people cc'd, and the question is for you personally — about your mistake. Reply all or just the sender?
The invite came three minutes before the start, and the link leads to last year's call, where a lonely security guard sits.
left: Skip it and get to work

text: You joined four minutes late. The host chirps: “Let me quickly recap for the latecomers” — and starts from the very beginning.
Coworkers in another time zone scheduled a call for 7 a.m. your time. “That works for you, right?”
right: Get up at 6:30 for the call

text: New tradition: standing stand-ups. Literally. The camera must show you standing, not sitting on the couch.
Someone created a chat called “URGENT!!! Project X,” added forty people, and wrote “Hi all.” No second message for an hour now.
Your morning calendar is empty, and someone already grabbed 8:30 for a “quick coffee call.” Block the morning as focus time?
At stand-up you learn the task you've worked on all week was closed long ago. It was announced in a channel you've muted.
A notification wakes you. At 6:40 a.m. the boss sent: “Got a minute?” Nothing else. Reply now?
An 80-person all-hands call. The host suggests “everyone briefly introduce themselves.” You're number sixty-three.
Stand-up now opens with a “mood check-in on a scale of 1 to 10.” Your honest number today is three.
Email from the boss: “Review before the 10:00 meeting.” Attached: a 94-slide deck. It's 9:40.
A coworker messages you “Hi” and goes quiet. The “typing…” indicator has been blinking for five minutes. Your move?
The executive's assistant reschedules your meeting for the fourth time: “How about tomorrow at 8 a.m.? No other slots.”
You arrive at the meeting room, but everyone else joined online from offices next door. Go back to your desk?
Stand-up has started, but the host is missing. Eight people silently stare at each other in little boxes. Take over?
It's 10:15 and there's no “Good morning, getting started” from you in chat. The boss has hearted everyone else's.
Your email suggests quick replies: “Sure, will do!”, “Great!”, “Thanks!” The email asks you to redo the entire project.
You open yesterday's meeting notes. They contain one line: “Agreed on everything.” Nobody remembers on what exactly.
A project teammate added you, without asking, to a daily series called “Just Chatting” through the end of the year.
The morning meeting opens with “Let's wait while everyone joins.” They've been waiting for twelve minutes.
The team lead wants you to post your update in chat before stand-up, then read it aloud at stand-up. Just to be safe.
right: Post it and read it aloud

text: Morning call, and your internet decided to transmit only every third word. And you need to say something important.
left: Type it in the call chat

text: An email arrives: “New Email Formatting Guidelines.” Thirteen pages, mandatory font, signature, and subject line color.
You're sharing your screen, and a coworker's message pops up in the corner: “So, has Mr. Boring joined yet?” Mr. Boring has joined.
The meeting has run an hour and you still don't know why you were invited. They're discussing another team's budget. What now?
Brainstorm: “There are no bad ideas!” You pitch an idea. The host: “Great. Except that one, of course.” What next?
Someone hit “Reply All” on a 600-person mailing list. Now everyone is replying all: “Take me off this list!”
You're munching a sandwich on a call, thinking your camera is off. It's been on for ten minutes, and everyone can see.
“Can you hear me?” “Yes.” “How about now?” “Yes.” “And now?” Round five. The agenda hasn't moved.
The host asks someone to take notes. Everyone in their little boxes suddenly looks very intently past the camera.
Someone booked your lunch hour with a “Lunch meeting: strategy discussion.” Judging by the description, no food will be provided.
The meeting ended with “Great, so we're agreed.” Judging by the faces, nobody understood on what exactly.
You click a meeting link and land in Legal's private meeting. Nobody has noticed you yet. What do you do?
Your department head on a call: “Let's all turn cameras on, I want to see faces.” His own camera is off.
You typed “Here he goes with his charts again” in the wrong chat. That chat includes “him.” The message has been read.
The CEO reacted to your report in the company chat with a clown emoji. Probably a misclick. Probably.
An hour-long meeting finished its agenda in ten minutes. The host: “Since we have time, let's brainstorm!”
Retro board: forty sticky notes under “What went badly,” one under “What went well” — “Pizza.” Add a note?
Mid-call, your cat strolls into frame and lies down on the keyboard. The team perks up for the first time in an hour.
You've been added to the chat “Gift for Accounting.” Sixty messages about how much to chip in, and zero decisions.
right: Propose an idea and a vote

text: Important call with leadership, and a “potato” filter switched itself on. Nobody knows how to turn it off.
right: Lead the meeting as a potato

text: Ideas go on the virtual whiteboard anonymously. Within a minute everyone recognizes your idea by your trademark typos.
right: Own it and take a bow

text: The thread has become “RE: RE: FW: RE: Fwd: RE: question.” Nobody remembers what the question was anymore.
right: Call a meeting, close it out

text: You forgot to mute and sighed loudly right as the boss said, “And just one more little thing.”
New chat rule: the “eyes” emoji means “seen.” Someone sent you nine files, and everyone's waiting for the eyes.
A coworker asks to “hop on a quick five-minute call” instead of typing one question in chat.
You're sharing a spreadsheet on a group call and notice the next column shows the whole team's salaries.
The organizer forgot to add the meeting link. Twelve people in the chat take turns writing “where's the link?”
You're running a meeting, and right now your neighbor starts drilling the wall. Directly behind you.
left: Hand it off to a coworker

text: You got notes from a meeting you didn't attend. According to them, you took on three tasks.
You're holding a tray in the cafeteria when the call comes: “Hop on for a sec, it's about your part.” Join from the cafeteria?
Your messenger status has said “At lunch” since last Thursday. Coworkers joke about the longest lunch in history.
A meeting with no agenda, and someone suggests “going around the room so everyone can speak.” You're seventh of twenty.
You're hosting an internal webinar. In half an hour, the chat has one question: “Will there be a recording?”
right: Add a quiz and a poll

text: You need to share your screen, and your desktop has 340 files named “final_FINAL_really_final_2.” Share as is?
6:45 p.m. The boss writes in chat: “We'll discuss tomorrow.” No context, no topic. Your evening is officially in question.
5:55 p.m. An invite for a “Quick Sync” at 6:00. The organizer is already online and waving cheerfully.
End-of-sprint retro. The host asks for one thing we should stop doing. “Calls” is right on the tip of your tongue.
Evening debate in the company chat over where to hold the holiday party. Three hundred messages. You get tagged: “What do you think?”
right: Weigh in and join the fight

text: The email is sent, and you spot a typo in the greeting: “Dear Mr. Petrvo.” Send a correction?
End of the day. You need to write up notes from a two-hour meeting. Your notes say only “important!!!” plus a doodle of a boat.
6:20 p.m. Coworkers in chat are planning a “quick call at 8:00” tomorrow. Object now or wake up at 7:30?
You set your status to “Do not disturb,” but the boss writes: “I see the green dot, answer me for a minute.”
A two-hour meeting ends with “Let's meet again.” You're asked to organize the next one.
5:40 p.m. Email: “Not urgent, but please reply today.” That's the twenty-second email like this today.
Closing your laptop, you notice you've been in someone else's call since 10 a.m. Camera off. Microphone — not.
A two-hour evening “Week in Review” call. Most of it is spent discussing how there are too many meetings.
6:30 p.m. You've been added to “Work Stuff (Casual).” A minute later: “So, heading home?” and “Who's finishing the report?”
Before leaving, you see tomorrow's calendar: “1:1 with manager. Topic: let's talk.” Not a word of detail.
A “quick half-hour” brainstorm at 5:30 turned into a fight over naming the project “Phoenix” or “Phoenix 2.0.” It's 6:40.
Everyone's gone, and your question in team chat has hung unanswered since 11 a.m. Under it: four “+1”s. Nobody knows.
5:50 p.m. Your calendar cheerfully reminds you: “Prepare materials for the 5:00 meeting.” The meeting is over.
You've typed a long message in the team chat about how badly everything is organized. Your finger hovers over “Send.”
The assistant sent out a poll: “Rate today's meeting from 1 to 5.” The poll, it turns out, isn't anonymous.
You sent your report in the evening and noticed the attachment isn't the report — it's a photo of your lasagna. It went to the whole team.
The boss asks “whoever missed it to watch the recording tonight.” It's 2 hours 40 minutes, no timestamps.
Your inbox says: “You have 0 unread.” For the first time in a year. You want to screenshot it for the team chat.
At 5:30 an “optional” meeting starts where, rumor has it, next week's tasks will be handed out.
The intern asks in the team chat how to mute notifications after 6 p.m. Everyone's silent, waiting for what you'll say.
6:05 p.m. You're in your jacket when your laptop pops up: “The boss is inviting you to a video call.” It's ringing.
Evening call with contractors: every other one says “Let me share my screen” and spends five minutes hunting for the button.
Your message in the company chat was read by 47 people. Zero replies. The question was “Who took my mug?”
You left a comment on a shared doc, and there are already twenty replies. Notifications keep pouring in at home.
The daily evening “Wrap-Up” call exists to announce that we'll wrap up tomorrow.
right: Show up and say a few words

text: Before leaving, you check tomorrow: nine meetings back to back, no window for lunch. Cancel something?
7 p.m. You're home, and the boss answers your question in the team chat with a six-minute voice message. Listen now?
At retro they suggest “publicly thanking one coworker.” Cameras are on, and everyone's waiting to hear who you'll name.
Evening. Someone in the team chat accidentally sent “Love you, pick up bread.” Everyone's reacting. Join in?
Notes from the afternoon meeting arrive at 6:50 p.m. with “Please approve by 7:00.” They're nine pages long.
Today is officially “No Elevator Day”: the company cares about your health. The office is on the 14th floor, and the elevator is taped off with a bow. How do you go up?
left: Wait by the elevator, just in case

text: They say whoever puts a new jug on the water cooler in the morning gets no bonus all quarter. The jug sits untouched while the line of empty mugs grows. Risk it?
right: Change the jug out of spite

text: The office moves on Friday, and boxes are handed out today: three per person. Your desk holds about eleven boxes’ worth of junk. What now?
Pigeons built a nest right on the AC unit. Turn it on and you evict a family. Don’t, and by lunch it’ll be 85 degrees in the office.
left: Sweat it out for the chicks

text: “A commercial is being filmed in the office today. Please look happy and don’t walk into the shot with mugs.” You’re standing at the entrance holding a mug. Your move?
left: Hide in the archive all day

text: By tradition, the new hire brings pastries on day one. Today’s new hire is the CEO, and nobody told him about the tradition. Your coworkers are looking at you.
The neighbors started a renovation overnight. The hammer drill kicks in exactly when someone says something important. It’s 9:00, and it’s warming up.
Starting today, everyone greets each other with “Good morning, colleague, it’s a great day for KPIs!” A secretary with a notepad at the door will be checking.
left: Just say “hi” like a normal person

text: A cat has moved into the office. No one knows whose it is or how it got past security. It’s asleep on your keyboard, typing “ffffffffff” into the team chat.
left: Work from your phone, let it sleep
right: Shoo the cat off the keyboard

text: A drill is announced: for half an hour, the office works “under blackout conditions,” by candlelight. Facilities brought the candles. Scented. Vanilla. Are you in?
left: Evacuate to the café across the street
right: Work by candlelight like a poet

text: Legend says if you boot up before the chief accountant, the day goes smoothly. She arrives at 7:30. It’s 7:29, and you reach the door at the same time.
left: Let her go first like a gentleman

text: A courier delivered a live baby goat in your name. The slip says: “A gift to the department from our partners, symbol of the year.” The goat is already chewing someone’s badge.
right: Sign for it, make it the mascot

text: It’s a month until New Year’s, but the tree is already up. Assignment: everyone hangs an ornament related to their job. Yours is “reporting specialist.”
“The ergonomics committee is here today. Sit up straight.” The committee is one very serious man with a protractor. He’s already heading to your desk.
right: Keep a straight back all day

text: Security has a new “morning alertness test”: name three rhymes for the word “report.” The entire Accounting department is breathing impatiently behind you.
A man in a bee costume has been sitting in reception since morning. He says he has a meeting “with whoever’s in charge of honey.” The receptionist is on vacation, and you’re closest.
right: Find whoever’s in charge of honey

text: Per the new memo, everyone brings a plant on Mondays “so the office can breathe.” It’s Monday, and all you have at home is a cactus and green onions in a jar.
left: Bring the onions in a jar
right: Buy a ficus on the way

text: The department has a “lucky pen”: no contract signed with it ever gets lost. Today the pen is gone, and everyone is eyeing each other suspiciously.
Every morning at exactly 9:00, a pigeon taps on the window like an alarm clock. Your coworkers think it’s a good-luck charm. Today Facilities brought anti-bird netting.
left: Let them put up the netting

text: The office moved, but your GPS stubbornly takes you to the old address, now a shawarma joint. The owner already recognizes you and waves. Going in?
Today is “Desk Swap Day”: everyone sits at the desk across from theirs. Yours belongs to a cactus fanatic, and it looks like a desert.
A guest book with a pen on a string has appeared in the restroom. Overnight it got twenty entries and a three-part poem. Will you contribute?
right: Add a stanza to the poem

text: The electrician says that at 10:00 half the floor will lose power, but he doesn’t know which half. The department is already taking bets. Where will you work?
left: Hide out in a café till lunch
right: Drag your laptop to the window

text: Mandatory morning exercises to a marching tune at 9:05 are now a thing. Half the department is hiding behind the archive shelves, waving at you: there’s room.
right: Work out in the front row

text: The office has a gong now: it’s struck at 9:00 to start the workday. According to the schedule, today it’s your turn. The mallet weighs as much as a dumbbell.
left: Hand the mallet to a neighbor

text: They say at 9:13 in elevator two you can meet the ghost of the former sales director, whispering the numbers of next year’s plan. It’s 9:12.
left: Take the stairs, just in case
right: Ride it and write down the numbers

text: New photo badges are being issued. Yours uses the picture from your HR file twelve years ago, with a haircut best forgotten. What do you do?
It’s Halloween and there’s a costume contest. In the elevator you ride with a vampire, a mummy, and a guy dressed as a quarterly report. You’re in a regular sweater.
right: Build a costume out of tape

text: It’s the 256th day of the year, Programmer’s Day. IT demands everyone greet each other in binary and hands out cheat sheets of ones and zeros.
For International Women’s Day, the team decided to skip the usual tulips and give people what they really dream of. You drew the chief accountant, who dreams of silence.
For Defender of the Fatherland Day, it was decided to congratulate the entire office, all eighty people, with one gift. Figuring out what it should be fell to you.
A note from the cleaners in the kitchen: “Whoever hid $5 in the flower pot, please take it, we don’t take what isn’t ours.” That’s your secret stash. Own up?
right: Take it in front of everyone

text: New memo: meetings are held standing, and the most important ones on one leg, “for focus.” The first important meeting is today at 9:30.
right: Stand on one leg to the end

text: There’s an envelope on your desk: “You have been chosen as Keeper of the Key to Room 404.” Key enclosed. There’s no Room 404 on this floor, but someone keeps locking it.
left: Turn the key in at reception

text: The workers next door accidentally punched a hole right into your office. Through it you can see their lunch and hear their radio. The foreman offers to share his pilaf.
left: Cover the hole with a poster

text: A pipe burst in the ceiling of the Neptune meeting room, and it’s literally raining inside. The partner meeting is in five minutes, and no rooms are free.
An audit from HQ has arrived. The inspector peeks into desk drawers and asks why you have fourteen packets of ketchup in yours.
Clearing out an old cabinet, you find a tin box labeled “Do not open until 2030.” Something rattles inside. Open it?
A stack of old, discontinued bills was found in Accounting’s cabinet. The accountant suggests donating them to the city museum or splitting them up “as souvenirs.”
A TV crew rented your floor as a “typical office.” The director asks you to play yourself, only “a little more tired.”
left: Go work in the supply closet

text: The corgi a coworker brought in “just for the day” dragged your lunchbox under the desk and is growling. The owner is at an offsite until evening. Lunch is in danger.
A talent show is announced. Your only talent: finding any file in the shared folder in under a minute. Sign-ups close in an hour. Are you in?
Accounting’s old printing calculator turns on by itself. Today it printed your employee ID and the amount “+$300.” Accounting is crossing themselves.
right: Demand the bonus per the tape

text: Thanks to a typo in a memo, instead of a drill “in case of an inspectors’ visit,” there’s a drill “in case of an aliens’ visit.” Security decided to run it as written.
left: Slip out to lunch in the chaos

text: The pigeons on the windowsill learned your message notification sound and repeat it every five minutes. You’ve checked your phone twenty times already. What now?
right: Feed them so they shut up

text: New policy: internal documents must be written in verse “to boost engagement.” You urgently need a memo about a broken chair.
right: Compose an ode to the chair

text: An elderly man in reception says he left an umbrella in this building in 1987 and has come to pick it up. His description of the umbrella is very detailed. Help him?
Painters are repainting the hallway and ask everyone to walk “only on the newspapers.” The newspapers are laid out so the trip to the restroom takes seven minutes.
Department law: whoever breaks a mug buys a cake. Your mug just cracked on its own — in the hands of someone from the next department over. Whose cake is it?
right: Demand a cake from the culprit

text: The head of Facilities brought a parrot “for morale.” It knows one phrase: “It’s not urgent.” They want to put the cage by your desk.
A photographer is here for the corporate website. You got cast as “a person who believes in synergy,” gazing thoughtfully into the distance with a tablet.
Something rustles in the ceiling above your desk, and this morning a note fell out: “Don’t touch the server room. Yours, the Fan.” Will you investigate?
The safety committee measured the lighting. Your workspace was deemed “excessively bright.” They propose hanging a sock on your lamp, per regulations.
Marketing’s hamster escaped its cage. It was last seen near your computer tower, and there’s a suspicious crunching of wires coming from it.
left: Wait for it to come out

text: There’s a contest to name the new meeting room. In the lead: “Nothing Gets Decided Here.” In second: “Horizon.” Voting is public, with names.
The movers mixed up boxes during the move. You got Purchasing’s folders, and your documents, according to the inventory, went to a warehouse out of town.
left: Wait for them to come back

text: An “anonymous ideas box” has been set up. Anonymity is guaranteed, but there’s a camera above the box and an employee with a notepad sitting next to it. Any ideas?
All day, the same ’90s song has been playing on repeat from the air vent. The department is singing along in chorus, and your spreadsheet is on fire.
A partner delegation arrived for a “how everything works here” tour. You’re the guide, it starts in ten minutes, and there’s no tour plan.
left: Hand the tour to the intern
right: Give a tour of office legends

text: Renovators found a niche behind the drywall: an old china set, a jar of jam, and 1979 quarterly reports. The reports balance to the penny. What do you do with the find?
right: Throw a tea party with the china

text: A courier brought forty “Congratulations, Valery!” balloons to your floor. There isn’t a single Valery in the office, and the courier is gone. The balloons are blocking the hallway.
right: Find Valery, even a floor down

text: The plumber has been fixing the water cooler for three hours, telling you his life story. Leaving is scary: unsupervised, he “also fixes” the coffee machine.
left: Leave and risk the coffee machine

text: The company next door accidentally invited your department to its team-building day with an escape room and lunch. It starts in an hour. Saying no is awkward, and work is piling up.
A “wishing tree” went up in the lobby: the CEO promises to grant one random wish. The branches already hold three notes saying “quit” and one saying “vacation forever.”
After the remodel, the doors lead to the wrong places: the kitchen opens into the server room, and the shortcut to the restroom goes through the CFO’s office.
The department is running a pool on which day the elevator breaks again. The security guard is taking bets, and the pot is up to three cakes. Want in?
The company commissioned a bust of the founder for the lobby. The founder is busy and asked the sculptor to “find someone who looks like me.” That’s you. Posing takes three hours.
5:45 p.m. The guard tells you in confidence that after six, someone shuffles folders in the archive. The cameras show nothing but an empty room and a falling stapler.
The New Year’s party is being held right in the office at 6:00 p.m. You got the role of Santa: the costume turned up, and the beard smells like mothballs.
6:10 p.m. The move is tomorrow, and nobody packed the three hundred potted plants. The elevator only goes down. The office manager looks at you hopefully.
Halloween night. Coworkers set up a horror escape room in a dark meeting room. The scariest thing inside is a note: “Next Year’s Annual Plan.”
6:30 p.m. In the empty Accounting office, the printer prints on its own: “The quarterly reconciliation doesn’t balance. Help.” It looks like the former chief accountant’s handwriting.
In the evening the pigeons fly off, and a huge crow lands on the windowsill, staring intently at your sandwich. It seems to have memorized your face.
They say whoever turns off the office lights last gets a promotion. Or a new project. It’s 6:55 p.m., there are three of you, and nobody is planning to leave.
The crew next door starts work at exactly 6:00 p.m., when everyone goes home. You have an evening report, and at 6:01 the angle grinder fires up.
The office talent show finale. The act before you juggles staplers and the crowd roars. Your act: a dramatic reading of an internal memo.
right: Read the memo like a tragedy

text: 5:50 p.m. The HQ committee asks you to “just sit with us while we flip through.” Judging by the stack, they’ll be flipping until about nine.
In the evening, a seven-foot teddy bear is delivered. The tag has your name and says: “From a secret admirer of your reporting.” Where do you put it?
left: Seat it in a meeting room
right: Take it home on the subway

text: Thursday evening tradition: at 6:00 p.m. everyone trash-talks the week in chorus, and the loudest gets the last cookie. It’s Thursday, and a lot has built up.
The office turns ten, and tonight a time capsule is opened in the lobby. Inside is your letter from the past, with predictions no one should ever hear.
The evening janitor found a box of lunchboxes forgotten over the years behind the coffee machine. He suggests a “night of memories” and opening them all.
At 6:00 p.m. there’s a drill on rescuing valuable property: everyone carries the most valuable thing out of the office. What’s worth more — your laptop or a coworker’s cactus?
There’s a hatch under your desk that even Facilities doesn’t know about. It’s 6:20 p.m., everyone is leaving, and the smell of fresh pastries is drifting up from it.
Tonight a show about “the most productive companies” is being filmed in the office. You’re asked to look frantically busy in the background until 9:00 p.m.
A pigeon arrives at the window with a note on its leg: “Sales on the fifth floor asks for its chairs back.” The pigeon awaits a reply and is in no hurry.
right: Write a reply and send it
