text: The stray cat the office fed all day refuses to leave in the evening and has settled into your bag. It’s purring and won’t give up your keys.
6:00 p.m. The holiday desk-decorating contest. Your neighbor has a paper-clip Christmas tree, Accounting has a garland of receipts. Your desk is still bare.
right: Build a tree out of folders

text: At 6:40 p.m. a man in a sea captain’s uniform walks in and asks where the “round-the-world voyages department” is. Security has already left.
They say if you leave a cookie on your desk overnight for the Accounting ghost, all the reports will balance by morning. It’s your last cookie, and you’re hungry.
The watchman locks up at 7:00 p.m. and today decided “not to check if anyone’s still here.” You’re still on the floor, it’s 6:58, and your report isn’t saved.
right: Spend the night in the office

text: The last evening in the old office. Coworkers suggest leaving a secret message on the wall for the next tenants. There’s a marker, and Facilities has gone home.
Evening email: tomorrow an auditor is coming “who could be anyone.” By morning everyone will suspect each other, but for now they suggest getting ready.
right: Stay late and clean your desk

text: The building manager announced the water would be shut off at 6:00 p.m. Everyone found out at 5:59, and you’re standing at the sink with soapy hands.
Superstition: never say “quiet evening” before 7:00 p.m., or something will break. The new guy just said it out loud, and the light flickered.
An employee art show opens in the lobby. Your doodle on a meeting napkin is hung front and center, titled “Despair. Ballpoint pen.”
left: Take it down and disown it

text: The founder’s bust has vanished from the lobby. Security asks everyone to stay and write down where they were since 5:00 p.m. You spent the whole evening at the coffee machine.
On the last day of the month, the department sings the company anthem written by a former marketer. It has forty verses, and the karaoke is already on.
At the end of the day, they raffle off “the right to skip stand-ups for a day.” A ticket costs one completed task for a coworker. The task takes two hours.
right: Do the task for a ticket

text: At the end of the hall is a door: “Long-Range Planning Department.” The light is always on, but no one has ever come out. It’s 6:30 p.m., and the door is ajar.
A Wednesday evening volunteer cleanup is announced: spruce up the flower bed by the office building. The flower bed is one tire and a concrete cat. Going?
The alarm goes off for the fifth time. “Five more minutes” has already eaten forty. Getting up?
In the mirror, a person with a pillow crease on their cheek shaped like a subway map stares back. Ten minutes until you leave.
The bus pulls up packed: people are squeezed so tight you don’t need to hold on. The next one is in twenty minutes.
The GPS shows a forty-minute jam and suggests a detour on a dirt road through a summer-cabin village. Risk it?
It’s pouring outside, and your umbrella has been living at the office since last Wednesday. A morning taxi costs as much as a mini-vacation.
left: Wait it out under an awning

text: You’re out of coffee at home. All that’s left is three-year-old instant with a proud label: “Vigor.” Drink it?
Monday. Your brain is still at the lake house; your body is already in the elevator. Dive in right away, or spend the first hour looking smart?
Your neighbor catches you at the elevator: “Is that your car under the window? Let’s talk about parking!” The elevator doors are already open.
The cat has curled up on the shirt you ironed last night and is purring loudly. The shirt is now fluffy. Move the cat?
The commuter train is fifteen minutes late. On the platform, someone is selling hot pastries with a mysterious filling. Buy one?
There’s a rental scooter by your building. Five minutes to the office on it, or twenty on foot. But the last time you rode one, you were a kid.
8:10 a.m. Mom calls to ask if you’re wearing a hat. It’s 60 degrees out. The conversation promises to be long.
The morning starts with a discovery: your neck won’t turn left. At all. And your monitor at the office is on the left.
left: Stay home with a heating pad
right: Go and turn your whole body

text: The hot water was shut off without warning. What comes out of the tap is very invigorating, about 46 degrees.
Making oatmeal takes ten minutes. Skip it, and by eleven you’ll be hunting other people’s cookies. Cooking?
A seat opens up in the car. Heading for it at the same time as you: a grandma with seedlings and a guy in headphones.
The bike in the hallway has been waiting for “a new life” for three weeks. There’s no shower at the office, and it’s 79 degrees out. Riding?
The new shoes look great, but they start quietly rubbing before you even leave the building. Going back for your old sneakers costs ten minutes.
Your eyes pop open at 4:47 a.m. on their own, no alarm. You’re wide awake, and it’s almost two hours until you have to get up.
left: Toss and turn till the alarm

text: Your phone didn’t charge overnight: the plug wasn’t all the way in. 4% battery, and an hour of commute ahead.
The elevator is broken, and you live on the twelfth floor. On the bright side, free morning cardio. Taking the stairs?
It snowed overnight, and your car is buried up to the mirrors. Your neighbor is already shoveling and offers to help — in exchange for a favor.
left: Ditch the car, take the bus

text: Stuck in traffic, the radio plays your favorite song from your youth. The driver in the next car is already singing. Belt it out?
Everything clean is gone. All that’s left is the reindeer sweater your aunt gave you for Christmas. It’s May.
right: Let the reindeer out in public

text: The dog demands its morning walk, and you’re already in your coat. It looks at you like you promised an hour in the park.
Your sister texts at 7:30: “Can you drop Tyoma off at daycare? It’s almost on your way.” The daycare is on the other side of the neighborhood.
You’re already at the subway, and your brain asks: did you turn off the iron? You don’t think you even own an iron. But what if.
A sweet nap on the bus, and now you’re at the end of the line. The driver kindly offers to take you back. Call the office?
You could get off a stop early and walk to the office through the park. Rumor has it there are squirrels.
A passing car splashes you from a puddle up to your waist. The office is two blocks away, home is five.
At exactly 7:00 a.m., your neighbor starts renovating. The hammer drill sounds like it’s boring straight through your pillow.
left: Endure with a pillow on your head

text: Working from home, 8:58 a.m. Shirt on top, penguin pajama pants on the bottom. In two minutes you need to turn on your camera.
right: Turn it on, penguins are off-screen

text: 6:30 a.m., a gorgeous sunrise outside. The running shoes you bought in January still have the tags on.
Your back is hinting: three hours without moving. A little longer and you’ll fuse with the chair. Stretch in the middle of the open office?
Your eyes are as dry as a quarterly report. There’s no distance to look into — just a wall with a fire extinguisher. Give your eyes a break?
Today the cafeteria has “home-style fish.” Whose home, no one knows. Next door, there’s a shawarma place with a half-hour line.
Your buckwheat and meatball from home are waiting to be reheated. There’s one microwave and a line of eight people with the same containers.
You found a chocolate bar of unknown vintage in your desk drawer. The expiration date has been erased by time. Eat it?
right: Eat it while no one’s looking

text: 3:00 p.m., post-lunch coma. Your eyelids weigh two pounds each. The meeting room is empty, and it has such a soft little couch.
A standing desk just freed up. They say it extends your life and shortens meetings. Give it a try?
Grandma calls in the middle of the day: the neighbor’s cat had kittens. Six of them, and one, she says, is “the spitting image of you.”
Your aunt sends a seven-minute voice message to the family chat. The first three minutes are about the weather. After that, maybe something important.
Working from home. The washing machine finished and beeps every two minutes. Hanging the laundry takes five minutes.
Working from home. Soup is simmering on the stove, and you’re deep in a task. Something suspiciously charcoal-like is wafting from the kitchen.
The cat walked across your keyboard and sent “asdfff////j” to the work chat. Everyone is politely waiting for an explanation.
During a call, your dog starts howling in unison with the presenter. You can’t mute: the mouse is under the dog.
right: Introduce the dog to the team

text: The sun is out for the first time in a month. The park is ten minutes away, lunch is forty. Go soak it up?
Your membership at the gym by the office is paid for the year. Visits: two. Today at lunch the gym is completely empty.
Reminder: dentist appointment today at 2:30 p.m. You booked it three months ago and successfully forgot about it.
left: Push it back three more months
right: Take time off for the dentist

text: A tab with flights is open “just to look.” Beach prices are suddenly quite reasonable. Buying?
First day back from vacation. 412 unread emails. The tan is still holding up; the mood already isn’t.
right: Delete all older than a week

text: The water bottle you filled this morning sits untouched. Meanwhile, your head is humming like a server room.
Spring: cottonwood fluff is drifting outside. A coworker wants to open the window, and you’ve sneezed twenty-three times already.
left: Put up with the open window

text: Forty pages left in your mystery novel, and the killer is about to be revealed. But coworkers are calling you to lunch in the cafeteria.
In the kitchen, people are discussing the latest episode of a show you haven’t seen yet. One word away from a spoiler.
A courier is delivering an order to your home “between 12 and 6.” No one’s home, and without you the package goes back to the warehouse.
By lunch, the letters on your monitor are blurring. Your glasses stayed home on the nightstand, next to your willpower.
Day three of a sugar-free month. On the next desk sits an open box of chocolates, quietly rustling its wrappers.
Your chair sank all the way down again. You look up at your monitor like it’s the starry sky.
right: Fix the chair for half an hour

text: Your stomach growls so loudly that your desk neighbor turns down his headphones. Lunch is an hour and a half away.
You yawn so widely it can be heard in the next office. Fifth time in ten minutes, and it’s contagious.
It’s 85 degrees in the office, and the AC has been “under repair” since June. You’re sticking to your chair. Roll up your sleeves and pants?
Working from home. The bed two steps away whispers: “Your laptop is portable. Work lying down.”
Your brother texts: “Help me pick a TV ASAP, I’m in the store, I have ten minutes.” And sends 14 photos of price tags.
By three o’clock, your step counter shows 412 steps. Some documents need to go up to the eighth floor. Elevator or stairs?
Your home camera shows the cat sitting on the fridge, slowly pushing your favorite mug toward the edge. While looking into the lens.
right: Yell at the cat via speaker

text: Your downstairs neighbors call: water is dripping from their ceiling. It seems to be yours. You’re at work across town.
5:55 p.m. Your gym bag has been staring at you from under the desk all day. Is the after-work workout still on?
Friends invite you to board games at 7:00 p.m. A game lasts “about two hours,” meaning until midnight. Tomorrow’s stand-up is at nine.
You need to stop at the store on the way home: all you have is mustard and hope. The checkout line stretches to the pasta aisle.
The new season of your favorite show dropped all at once: ten episodes. Tomorrow is a workday. Watch “just one”?
6:05 p.m. The GPS promises you’ll be home in 1 hour 40 minutes. You could wait out traffic at the office and clear your inbox.
Mom calls: “Coming this weekend? I need help with the potatoes.” And the weekend was planned to be strictly horizontal.
Your date is at 7:30 p.m., and you’re still at the office looking like a report draft. Can you make it home to change?
A 3,000-piece puzzle is waiting at home. All that’s left is the sky: eight hundred identical blue pieces.
The broccoli in the fridge has been waiting six days for a healthy dinner. The dumplings in the freezer aren’t judging.
The pile of dishes in the sink has become a sculpture. Wash them now, or call it contemporary art?
The plumber promises to come “between 6 and 9.” That means leaving at 5:30, and you still have three tasks.
6:00 p.m., your sister calls: “Masha has a school play tomorrow, she needs a snowflake costume. You can sew, right?” You can’t.
A warm evening. It’s forty minutes home on foot along the river, or fifteen by bus — and the bus is just pulling up.
6:40 p.m., you’re home in your slippers. Your phone lights up: 47 new messages in the work chat.
Before heading home, decide: alarm at 6:00 tomorrow to get everything done, or 7:30 to get nothing done again?
Friends invite you to their cabin overnight: barbecue, a sauna, and mosquitoes the size of your palm. Leaving tonight right after work.
Tonight is your second Italian class. The homework — talking about yourself — is still not done.
Leaving the office, you walk into pea-sized hail. The subway is fifteen minutes away; a taxi is promised in forty.
left: Wait in the lobby with security

text: You go to the store for bread, and there’s a deal: “Three pizzas for the price of two.” Pizza for dinner, pizza for breakfast, pizza for the office?
A flat-pack wardrobe awaits at home: 214 parts and an instruction manual without a single word. Assembly takes “about two hours.”
right: Build it to the bitter end

text: 6:50 p.m. Your third video in a row about how to get proper sleep. Naturally, this isn’t giving you any more sleep.
5:45 p.m. An hour left in the day, and your energy ran out at lunch. Look frantically busy, or honestly finish the small stuff?
After work, everyone’s going ice skating. Your skating experience: once, at age nine, very briefly.
You have 1,200 vacation photos on your phone. Tonight you could pick the best ones to show the team tomorrow. Or at least the funny ones.
The studio by the subway has a discounted back massage at 6:30 p.m. You can only book it right now, and tasks are still hanging over you.
The cat informs you the food ran out this morning. The pet store closes at 7:00 p.m., and you’re still at work.
There’s a bike rental in the park by the office. The sun is setting, the breeze is warm. And tomorrow at eight, a big report is due.
A high school classmate messages for the first time in ten years: “Let’s meet up tonight and reminisce!” You vaguely remember his last name.
Your guitar has been gathering dust in the corner for five years. The neighbors just left, and your fingers might still remember three chords.
A bubble bath and silence await at home. But Oleg from the team asks for help moving a couch: “It’s light, fifth floor, no elevator.”
Friends suddenly invite themselves over at eight. Your place is a mess, and your fridge echoes.
It’s warm at home, with a blanket and a cat on your lap. But in an hour, your friend’s birthday party starts at a bar across town.
The passport office closes at 7:00 p.m., and you can’t get your passport without that certificate. Vacation is in a month, and it’s 5:20 p.m.
9:05 a.m. Overnight, 14 tasks were assigned to you in the tracker. All are “Critical,” and one is “Critical+.” Where do you start?
Sprint planning. You’re asked to estimate in hours a task called “Do it right.” No description, just the title and three exclamation points.
To get a new pen, you must turn in your old, empty one and fill out a request form in duplicate. In pen. Filing it?
Your train for a business trip leaves tomorrow morning, and the trip authorization still isn’t signed. Without it, Accounting won’t pay per diem. Go anyway?
The archive is open from 9:00 to 9:15 a.m. It’s 9:12, and you need a 2019 folder from the basement. Run for it?
You made a perfect nine-item plan for the day. At 9:20, item number one becomes “redo yesterday’s work.” Rewrite the plan?
A new version of the approval policy is out. It’s 63 pages and took effect yesterday. Sign that you’ve read it by lunch.
The project folder has “report_final,” “report_final2,” “report_FINAL_really,” and “report_final2_new.” Which one went to the client yesterday?
They need a report on how much work time goes into reports. The format is a new 12-column spreadsheet, due by 10:00 a.m.
The morning starts with an inventory audit. The stapler on your desk has an asset tag, but the desk itself doesn’t. Tell the committee?
The project manager asks for a timeline estimate, “rough, totally non-binding.” Last time, such an estimate ended up in the contract.
Launching the project requires five signatures. Four signers are on vacation, and the fifth only signs after the first four. What now?
Morning status update. All of yesterday went into searching for a lost file, and the file was found. How do you describe your day?
Overnight, someone sorted just one column in the shared project sheet. Now task deadlines are mixed up with people’s names. Fix it?
Your travel expense report was rejected for the fifth time: the café receipt is “the wrong format.” The trip was in March. Keep fighting?
Time to enter quarterly goals into the system. You need at least five SMART goals. So far you have one: survive till Friday.
You’re inheriting a project from an employee who quit. All the documentation is a sticky note: “ask Oleg.” Oleg quit even earlier.
A new memo template was approved: different font, indent 0.2 inches larger. All of this week’s memos must be redone.
9:00 a.m. For the task you were told yesterday was “not before next week,” an email arrives: “Could we have it by lunch?”
The contract needs the blue stamp. The stamp is in the safe, the key is with the secretary, and the secretary is out sick until Thursday.
You have 27 cards in your “In Progress” column. The analyst suggests a rule: no more than three at once. Clean it up?
This morning, a memo renamed the department. Forms, email signatures, and the door sign all need redoing. In May, the department will be renamed back.
Backlog grooming. The oldest task is three years old, its author has long since moved to another company, but its status is still “Important.” Close it?
Buying $7 of tape requires a budget request approved by Finance, Legal, Security, and the deputy director. The tape is needed today.
left: Buy it with your own money

text: The sales proposal goes out at 10:00. At 9:40 you discover the logo is last year’s and the prices are from the year before.
The KPI report is in: 104% on tasks outside your job description, and 0% on the ones in it.
Outgoing letters get a reference number from a paper logbook in the records office on another floor. The letter itself is one line: “Thank you.”
Time to update the project roadmap. Every deadline on it has already passed, but you can’t delete them — “it’s history.” What do you do?
This morning you need to send out the minutes from yesterday’s meeting. Your notes contain one phrase: “Revisit this later.”
On a new project, the “Owner” field has your name. No one warned you, and you’re seeing the project for the first time.
Good news: the deadline moved. Bad news: two days earlier. The email says the reason is “it’s more convenient for reporting.”
The new document system: sign electronically, then print and sign with a pen “for the archive.” Do both?
Finance wants a three-year forecast for your project. Meanwhile, there’s still no plan whatsoever for the current month.
left: Pull numbers out of thin air

text: The corporate portal books your business trip on a 5:20 a.m. flight. Convenient flights are “outside travel policy.” Your call?
left: Pay for a better one yourself

text: The partner presentation must follow the brand guidelines. The brand book is 3 GB and contradicts itself on page 12.
You need to compile data from six departments. One sent it in dollars, another in thousands, a third as a photo of a notepad page.
To move your desk a foot and a half toward the window, you need a memo to Facilities with a justification and a diagram. Writing it?
Turns out you and someone from the next department have spent two weeks making the same report. Both are nearly done. Who submits?
A contractor sent a completion certificate. The work is 60% done; the certificate says 100%. It needs a signature today.
The file you worked on all morning has vanished. There is an autosave — from the Tuesday before last. What now?
Your neighbor asks you to “take a quick look” at his 80-page report and sign off by 3:00 p.m. Your sign-off is third on the approval list.
Estimating tasks. Everyone held up a “3” card; yours says “40.” The whole team is staring. Explain yourself or give in?
One cell with a “#VALUE!” error in your report drags 400 others down with it. In an hour, the report goes up the chain.
You fixed one comma in the contract. Per policy, that’s a new revision, and approval starts over: Legal, Finance, Security.
The committee is looking for monitor #00417. According to the records it’s yours, but the one on your desk is #00418. Investigate?
The business trip report requires event photos, boarding passes, and a three-page “statement of benefit to the company.”
The archive only accepts last year’s documents bound, numbered, and with an index. Turns out they needed binding since January.
Task in the tracker: “Do it the way we discussed.” It was discussed verbally, a month ago, by three people, and everyone remembers it differently.
Legal sent a contract with edits, but track changes was off. Spot the differences: 47 pages of fine print.
A partner department asks you to add another phase to your project “within the current budget.” There’s $40 left in the budget.
To get a new laptop, you need nine signatures from six different floors. The elevator is out until Monday.
You have to fill out a whole month's timesheet retroactively. All you remember is that there was a lot of work.
right: Rebuild it from email and chat

text: Someone is typing right over your section of the shared doc. The cursor says “Anonymous 4,” and your work is vanishing before your eyes.
You've been added to a working group drafting a policy on how to write policies. The first session starts right now.
right: Go and pitch your own draft

text: To pick up a package of documents, you need a power of attorney. To get the power of attorney, you need the documents in the package.
left: Wait for it to sort itself out

text: You're asked to review a report that reviews another report. There are errors in all three documents.
left: Send it back to all three authors

text: A third of every slide in the corporate template is taken up by the motto “Together Toward Results.” There's no room for the chart.
right: Squeeze the chart into a corner

text: The spec template requires both a “Glossary” and a “Terms and Definitions” section. Nobody in the office knows the difference.
The master file of the quarterly plan is open by 17 people at once. Every save breaks it and offers to “recover.”
Accounting needs the original invoices by 4 p.m., or the payment slips to next month. The originals are at your place.
The rollout of the new task-tracking system is behind schedule. Someone suggests opening a ticket “Speed up rollout” — in the old system.
They want the report “as an editable PDF, but so nobody can edit it.” Due by 3 p.m.
The weekly report has a field: “What's getting in the way of your work?” The three people who wrote “the weekly report” got called in for a talk.
The report you already sent to the director shows revenue ten times higher than reality. The director hasn't replied yet.
The records clerk wants you to assign a file category to your correspondence. You have to pick from a list of 340 options.
Turns out the task you've spent three days on was canceled back on Monday. They just forgot to tell you.
Your team lead wants a Gantt chart for a two-hour task. “For process transparency.”
5:55 p.m. An email arrives: “Could we have this by tomorrow?” with a 40-page attachment. The sender has already gone home.
The report must be uploaded to the portal by 6 p.m. At 5:58, the portal says “Session expired.” The password was changed this morning.
6:10 p.m. The director is ready to sign — but only right now, and only on paper. The printer on this floor is already off.
Evening. All your tickets are closed, but the chat asks you to “grab one more small one, since you're free anyway.”
6:30 p.m. “report_final_FINAL” is sent. A minute later, new edits arrive with the subject “last ones.” That's the fifth “last ones” today.
Last day to submit your expense report. You're missing a $5 lunch receipt. It's probably in your jacket pocket — and the jacket's at the dry cleaner.
7 p.m. Slides for tomorrow morning's talk are 80% done. All that's left is the “Conclusions” slide, but there are no conclusions yet.
You find the archive room key in your pocket. Rules say it goes back to security by 6 p.m. It's 6:20.
6:05 p.m. The time sheet has to be closed today. According to the system, you've been on vacation since last Wednesday.
5:50 p.m. Someone at a branch office assigns you a task “by end of day.” Their day ends in six hours — different time zone.
left: Do it in the morning, your time

text: In the evening, you realize the invoice you signed has the wrong amount on it. Accounting already has their copy.
6:40 p.m. The annual report file won't save: “Insufficient permissions.” You had permissions this morning.
right: Save to a USB and email it

text: Evening. They want an hour-by-hour plan for next week. Half the week is “waiting for approval.”
Business trip. Your train leaves in two hours, but your hosts won't let you go without a signed report — in triplicate.
5:30 p.m. Someone moved your deadline in the project calendar to 9 a.m. tomorrow with the note “has to be this way.” Unsigned.
The audit is tomorrow. Tonight you learn that half the documents were signed in blue ink, but the manual says purple.
6:15 p.m. A reminder about the monthly report nobody reads. If you skip it, the reminder goes to your manager.
To close the project in the tracker, you must fill 22 required fields. “Lessons learned” needs at least 500 characters.
Your trip report needs an arrival confirmation stamped by the host company. The host company is in another city.
right: Ask them to send a scan

text: 6 p.m. Ten minutes of work left on the task. But after 6:01 it's overtime, which needs a request approved in advance.
Cleaning your desktop before leaving, you delete the folder “DO NOT DELETE!!!” The recycle bin is already empty, too.
left: Act like it was always so

text: 6:20 p.m. The CEO wants a report “on one page.” You have 30 pages, and all of it matters. How do you cut it?
Evening — time to send the weekly project digest. Nothing happened this week except three deadline slips.
6 p.m. You're asked to sign meeting minutes backdated to last month. “It's just a formality, everybody does it.”
The report is done, but your inner voice whispers: “Double-check the formulas.” That'll take two hours. Listen to it?
The courier picks up documents at 6 p.m. They won't be accepted without Legal's sign-off, and the lawyer's been silent since lunch.
right: Hunt the lawyer floor by floor

text: You have to submit a memo on the need to reduce the number of memos. In triplicate.
5:45 p.m. A ticket gets reassigned to you, and its status flips to “Overdue.” The deadline was 5:44.
Evening. You need to reconcile the badge log with reality. 112 rows, forty of them with the last name Smith.
6 p.m. Tomorrow's business trip is canceled. Now the tickets, hotel, and travel order all need canceling — via three separate forms.
6:30 p.m. Last hour to enter data for the quarterly report. Last quarter's numbers match this quarter's suspiciously exactly.
Thursday evening. To hit Friday's deadline, you could take work home. But laptops only leave with a property removal pass.
The report from the partner department finally arrived. No program in the office can open its format. Now what?
Every morning your desk neighbor parks his mug on your side. Today there are three mugs and a spoon crusted in sugar. Return the whole collection?
7:40 a.m. and the department chat already has 58 messages about who didn't clean the coffee machine. Everyone's a suspect, including you. Jump in?
Intern Timofey showed up at 7:30, though the day starts at nine. He's waiting at the door with a notebook: “So what do I do today?”
right: Give him a task and explain

text: Sveta brought homemade pancakes for the whole department and is watching who takes how many. Your diet started Monday. It's Wednesday. Take one?
The new hire asks where to sit. The only free spot is next to you — covered by your coat, umbrella, and strategic cookie reserve. Clear it?
Zina is going around with an envelope: a birthday collection for a guy in Logistics. You saw him once, by the elevator, and he didn't say hi. How much?
Igor is forty minutes late and whispers: tell the boss he's “been here ages, just in a meeting room.” The boss is walking right toward you. Cover for him?
Your desk neighbor starts the day with workouts right at his desk: squats, bends, loud exhales. He waves at you: “Come on, join me!” Will you?
Someone accidentally sent a four-minute voice message to the group chat — clearly meant for their mom. It's about seedlings, the mortgage, and maybe you. Listen?
Marina announces she just broke up with her boyfriend and sits down with you “for five minutes.” It's 9:05, and you have a whole morning to-do list. Listen?
The smokers invite you to “just hang out” with them outside — that's where everything gets decided before stand-up. You don't smoke, and it's 14°F out. Go?
The intern brought everyone coffee but mixed up the orders. You got a salted caramel pumpkin latte, and he's looking at you hopefully. Drink it?
Every morning Tamara Petrovna turns on a radio morning show. The hosts have been cracking up at their own jokes for an hour. You haven't laughed once. Offer headphones?
Denis booked your favorite meeting room for the whole morning to “work in peace.” Through the door, you can hear him watching a medical drama. Knock?
Your shift partner left a note: “Didn't quite finish, you'll figure it out.” “Didn't quite” means three folders and one very angry logbook. Now what?
left: Return the note with a reply

text: Vera brought a kitten to the office because there's “nobody to leave it with.” The kitten is now fast asleep on your keyboard. Wake it up?
Someone shoved your soup to the back of the fridge and put a jar in its place labeled “Don't touch. This is a test.” Nobody admits what's being tested. Move it?
Pasha came in with a cold and proudly declared he “won't take sick leave, work comes first.” He sits three feet from you, sneezing into his hand. Send him home?
New hire Alina asks who in the department she can go to for help — and who's best avoided before lunch. Give her the unofficial map?
left: Point her to the org chart

text: Your desk neighbor turned his monitor so he can see your screen, and every five minutes he says, “Oh, you're in spreadsheets too.” Build a barrier?
It's your turn on the schedule to wash the office kettle and toss the mountain of tea bags. Lyosha offers to swap: he does today, you take his Friday. Deal?
Rita decided the team doesn't communicate enough and put up a “gratitude board.” So far there's one note — from Rita to herself. Write something?
Gena declared a “month without coffee.” Day two: he's yawning, cranky, and already fought with the printer. Your mug is steaming fragrantly. Support him?
Your best friend at work secretly tells you they're leaving for another company next month. Coworkers suspect something and are grilling you at the water cooler. Keep it?
Oksana from next door comes to “borrow” your stapler for the third time this week. The first two never came back. Lend another?
Vitalik started a chat poll: set the AC to 79°F or not? Five for, five against, and everyone's waiting for your tie-breaking vote. Your pick?
The intern confesses he accidentally deleted the shared department folder yesterday and begs you to restore it before the manager arrives. That's in twenty minutes. Save him?
It's Sasha's birthday today, but he's acting like it's a regular Tuesday. You found out by accident from the calendar. Tell the team?
Vasya borrowed your charger “for five minutes” and took it into a two-hour meeting. Your phone is at 4%. Go get it?
Nina arrives first and turns on every light, though you love the dim corner by the window. Today she also put a lamp on your desk: “You'll ruin your eyes.” Turn it off?
right: Switch it off and thank her

text: The department chat has a new morning ritual: everyone rates their mood from one to ten. Everyone has posted “7.” What do you post?
At stand-up, Artyom pitches the idea you two came up with yesterday at the water cooler. There's one name on the slide — his. Correct him in public?
right: Correct him in front of all

text: Ira is waiting at the entrance with two coffees: “You'll help me with my presentation today, right?” The coffee's already bought and getting cold. Take it?
right: Take the coffee and your fate

text: Kostya started morning “motivation minutes”: he reads quotes from great people and asks everyone to clap. Attendance is optional, but he's taking names. Go?
Your desk neighbor is eating yesterday's garlic fish at his desk. The smell reached the meeting room, and everyone's looking at you — you sit closest. Say something?
Lena asks you to “take a quick look” at her report before she sends it. It's thirty pages, and “quick” means by lunch. Take it on?
Galya whispers that the accountant and the IT guy have had lunch together three times now. “It's a romance, I'm telling you.” She awaits your reaction. Bite?
The team is ordering lunch together. Dima suggests “splitting it evenly,” though he got a steak and you got soup and bread. Push back?
Maxim from your own department grabbed the same task you're on, and now it's a race. He's already posted in chat: “Almost done.” Speed up?
Olya runs over with her laptop: “Be honest, is this dress okay for the office party?” On screen: bright lime green, with feathers and fringe. Be honest?
Roma perched on your desk to tell you about his renovation: tile, grout, spackle, more tile. It's been twenty minutes. Your move?
Sales wants to borrow your intern “for literally an hour” to hand out flyers at the entrance. The intern looks at you like a hostage. Let him go?
Zhanna is hosting a kitchen tasting of her new hobby: old-world pickled vegetables. The whole floor smells. She hands you a fork. Try some?
The chat has spent an hour arguing about whose turn it is to order water for the cooler. It's gotten personal — someone's sins from three years ago came up. Step in?
Tyoma asked you to cover for him for two hours for a “very important personal matter.” Half an hour later, his water park photos hit social media. Say something?
On day one, new guy Kirill got chummy with everyone and proposed overhauling the department's processes. The veterans are tense and watching you. Back him?
Vika is collecting $20 each for the department head's gift and already picked a grill set with skewers. The boss is a devout vegetarian. Object?
Your desk neighbor clicks his pen nonstop. Now he's clicking to the beat of some song, and you think you're starting to recognize it. Gift him a capped pen?
Natasha is getting married and handing out invitations — you got one too. The wedding is Saturday out of town, and your report is due Monday. Go?
Boris is loudly on the phone with his mother-in-law in the open space. The whole office now knows the summer house isn't selling and the cucumbers are bitter this year. Ask him out?
Filipp offers a swap: he takes your boring reconciliation, you take his “exciting” project with a trip to the warehouse. Sounds suspiciously generous. Agree?
Someone posted your photo from the office party two years ago — the one where you're dressed as a pumpkin. Already 14 reactions. Ask to delete or play along?
Tonya casually asks how much you make. “Just for statistics, I won't tell anyone.” Galya is lurking suspiciously behind her. Answer?
Misha was reheating buckwheat and caused a small explosion in the microwave. It's coated inside, and twelve hungry people are in line. Help clean?
Stas decided you're best friends and DMs you every ten minutes: memes, news, photos of his lunch. 47 messages today. Reply to even one?
Alla is going on maternity leave and handing her work to you. The handoff took fifteen minutes and one sentence: “It's all clear, call me if anything.” Will you call?
The team needs players for the interdepartmental ping-pong tournament. One spot left, and the last time you held a paddle was summer camp. Play for the team?
Timur accidentally forwarded you an email where he discusses your work with a friend from another department. The review is, to put it mildly, not glowing. Now what?
right: Forward it back with a question

text: The intern proudly brings you his first report. It's in a curly font, and the total is highlighted pink and circled with a heart. Be direct?
right: Go through it point by point

text: Your monitor is in the shop until Thursday. Rustam generously offers to share his: “You get the left half, I get the right.” Deal?
Polina is quietly crying in a meeting room: her vacation request for her sister's wedding got denied. You're the only one walking by. Go in?
Anya and Petya are clearly smitten: coffee runs together, inside jokes in chat. Anya asks how to invite Petya to a movie. Help her?
Lida is off on a business trip and lines your shared windowsill with twelve pots of seedlings. Tomatoes, peppers, and one suspicious cactus. Water them?
Every half hour your desk neighbor asks, “Do you know how to…?” — then something you could google in five seconds. That's nine today. What do you do?
Elvira brought a giant “Ocean Breeze” diffuser. An hour later, the whole office smells like a taxi air freshener. She's beaming: “Isn't it cozier now?”
Two coworkers fought over the window chair and haven't spoken in three days. Each asks you to pass along “just one thing” to the other. Be the mailman?
Yura wants you to come sneaker shopping on lunch: “I need an honest eye.” Lunch is an hour, and the store is forty minutes away. Go?
5:45 p.m. Dima invites everyone to karaoke after work: “Just one duet with me!” He's already picked a six-minute love ballad. Go?
Katya leaves at 5:00 sharp and asks you to “answer for her in chat if anything comes up.” It's come up three times in half an hour. Keep covering?
left: Say she's gone for the day

text: 6 p.m. A new collection in the team chat: a gift for a coworker who quit last month. “Well, she was nice.” Chip in?
right: Chip in and sign the card

text: Vova offers you a ride home, but with a “quick” stop at his mom's to pick up jars of pickles. There are “not many” jars, he says. Go?
6:20 p.m. Larisa is staying late and asks you to stay too: “It's scary alone in an empty office.” She has two more hours of work. Stay?
left: Leave and leave the lights on

text: At the end of the day, Taras hands out apples from his garden. Four sacks, and your bag is already full. Take ten pounds or so?
Alexey stops you at the door to show his “brilliant” 40-slide plan to optimize the department. You've already got your coat on. Watch it?
6:40 p.m. A scandal in the chat: someone ate someone else's yogurt. The accused went offline, the victim demands a vote. Vote?
At the end of the day, Lyuda leaves you a “small favor”: print and file two hundred forms for her morning event. She's already running for the elevator. Call after her?
left: Put them back on her desk

text: Gosha invites you to the gym on a guest pass: “Leg day, squats with a trainer.” Rumor has it the trainer is ex-military. Go?
Emma suggests walking to the subway together to “debrief the day”: who said what and who gave whom a look. The walk is ten minutes; the debrief is an hour. Go?
The new hire stays until nine every night to make an impression. Management is now asking why everyone else leaves at six. Talk to him?
5:30 p.m. Zoya is moving to a department two floors up and throws a farewell tea: tears, toasts, cake. As if she's moving to another continent. Stay?
left: Hug her and leave on time

text: Robert insists Friday's office party dress code is “80s retro” and has already bought a wig. Nobody else has heard of this. Back the idea?
Your shift partner asks you to stay half an hour: her son has a fever at daycare. Your bus leaves in fifteen minutes. Cover for her?
Anton suggests a Secret Santa without waiting for the holidays, just to lift spirits. Budget is $10, drawing names right now. In?
Before leaving, Yulia thanks you in front of everyone for saving her report. Except it was Seryozha who saved it — he's sitting right there, silently staring at you. Correct her?
5:55 p.m. Your desk neighbor starts packing up loudly: zippers, bags, heavy sighs. Everyone else glances at the clock and feels guilty. Leave with him?
Coworkers are planning a weekend camping trip: tents, guitar, mosquitoes. The list is done, and you're on it — in charge of the cooking pot. Confirm?
Rimma is staying late and sighs loudly in the empty office: “Of course, it's all on me again.” Nobody else is here but you. Offer help?
On the last day of his internship, the intern gives you a drawing of you with wings, captioned “Best Mentor.” Hang it over your desk?
Fyodor asks for help moving this weekend: “Not much — a couch, a wardrobe, and a piano.” He promises pizza and eternal gratitude. Help?
Inna invites you to evening Spanish classes: “More fun together, plus a refer-a-friend discount.” Three times a week, right after work. Sign up?
6:30 p.m. Savva calls: he left his apartment keys at work, and you're still in the office. He asks you to bring them across town. Go?
Zlata secretly tells you Oleg from Procurement is dating Veronika from Legal. A minute later, you see she's “secretly” told five more people. Warn Oleg?
6:10 p.m. Nikita says he's out tomorrow, so you're giving his morning presentation. He'll “send the slides tonight.” Wait for them?
An office couple is fighting by the elevator and wants you to judge: did he forget their anniversary, or did she remind him too often? The elevator arrives in a minute.
Stepan is retiring and on his last day asks you to take the cactus he grew in the office for twenty years: “Just keep it near a window.” Take it?
5:50 p.m. Ulyana asks you to look over her résumé: “Don't tell anyone, I'm just exploring options.” It's open right on her work computer. Help?
Marat came in late and left early, but posts in chat: “Rough day, folks, we worked our tails off.” The message has 12 sympathetic reactions. Reply?
On the way to the subway, Galya asks why you talked to the boss so long after lunch. “Promotion? Firing? You can tell me.” Tell her?
Lev started a Thursday book club after work. The first book: eight hundred pages on management philosophy, discussion in a week. Join?
At the end of the day, Regina gathered the team “for a minute” to pick who decorates for the holiday. It's been forty minutes. No volunteers. Step up?
Your laptop decided to install 47 updates at exactly 9:58. Stand-up is at 10:00. Wait it out or improvise?
left: Wait with a cup of tea

text: “Password expired. The new one can't match your last 24 and must contain a special character, a number, and a little pain.” Come up with one?
The VPN has been connecting for 12 minutes, the bar frozen at 99%. They say jiggling the cables under the desk helps. There are eight cables down there.
The sysadmin asks you not to turn on your computer until 11 a.m.: “maintenance in progress.” Maintenance has been in progress since last Thursday.
Your key card got demagnetized. The turnstile beeps, the guard hunts for the logbook, the line behind you sighs. How do you get in?
Your wireless mouse is dead: battery's out. Spares are locked in the facilities manager's cabinet until noon. But there's a remote in the meeting room.
The “o” key is stuck. Every email now looks like “Gd mrning, please apprve.” Fix it or call it good enough?
left: Type as is, they'll get it
right: Pry it open with a butter knife

text: After the weekend, your second monitor decided it's now the first. Windows slid left, and the cursor is lost somewhere off the desk.
You left your laptop charger at home, battery at 14%. The accountant has the same one, but she never lends it to anyone. Ever.
Email: “Your mailbox is full, enter your password at this link ASAP.” Sender: “Office Securty Sysadmin.” What do you do?
The AI offers to plan your day. Its plan: 9:00 — coffee, 9:15 — synergy, 9:30 — more coffee. Trust it?
The time-tracking system logged your arrival at 9:01 and marked the day red. The wall clock says 8:57. Dispute it?
Since morning, the cloud folder has been syncing 3,842 files. Yesterday's report is somewhere at the very end of the queue.
The intern needs access to the shared folder. Requests take five business days. The intern looks at you with kitten eyes.
right: Lend him your login for a day

text: Your digital signature certificate expired at midnight. Fourteen contracts must be signed by lunch. Go get a new one?
The office Wi-Fi password changed. The new one is on a sticky note in the meeting room — where the director has been in session all morning.
After an update, your laptop's camera light is on by itself. It's been half an hour. Who's watching you is unclear.
Your laptop clock says it's 2004. Because of that, no website will load and no email comes through. Fix it yourself?
Overnight, 214 unread messages in the work messenger. 200 are stickers in the “Random” channel. Somewhere in there, maybe, is a task.
